**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 1:**

(p-113)(5 Surat al-Ma'idah)

Medinan, and its number of verses is one hundred and twenty.

In the name of God, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿O you who have believed, fulfill the contracts.﴾ *Al-wafa'* is carrying out what the covenant requires. Likewise *al-iyfa'*. *Al-'aqd* is a firm covenant. Al-Hutay'ah said:

*A people who, when they make a covenant with their neighbor,*
*Tighten the 'inaj and tighten over it the karaba.*

Its origin is joining two things together in such a way that separating them is difficult. Perhaps what is meant by *al-'uqud* (the contracts) is that which encompasses the contracts God, glory be to Him, made upon His servants and obligated them to through the duties, and what they make among themselves of contracts of trust, transactions and the like, which must be fulfilled, or which is good if we take the command as common to both obligation and recommendation.

﴿Lawful for you is the beast of the grazing livestock﴾ is a specification of the contracts. *Al-bahimah* is every living creature that cannot discern. It is said: every four-footed creature. Its attribution to *al-an'am* (the grazing livestock) is for clarification, like your saying "a garment of silk" (*thawb khazz*), meaning "the beast from among the grazing livestock." These are the eight pairs. The gazelles are added to them, and the wild animals are also included. It is said: these are the intended meaning of "beast" and similar things that resemble the grazing livestock in chewing the cud and lacking fangs. Its attribution to the grazing livestock is due to the resemblance involved.

﴿Except what is recited to you﴾: except the forbidden part of what is recited to you, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Forbidden to you is carrion﴾. Or, except what is recited to you as its prohibition.

﴿Not violating the game while you are in the state of ihram﴾: this is a circumstantial clause (*hal*) from the pronoun in *lakum* (for you). It is said to be from the *waw* of *awfu* (fulfill). It is also said to be an exception, but this is strained. *Al-sayd* (the game) may be either a verbal noun or a passive object.

﴿While you are in ihram﴾: a circumstantial clause from the hidden pronoun in *muhillin*. *Hurum* is the plural of *haram*, meaning the one in a state of prohibition (ihram).

﴿Indeed, God decrees what He wills﴾: of permission or prohibition.

O you who have believed, do not violate the sacred rites of God, meaning the rites of the Hajj, the plural of sha'irah, which is the name for anything that is marked (ash'ara), that is, made a sign. The rites of the Hajj and its stations are called by this name because they are the signs of the Hajj and the markers of the rituals. It is also said that it means the religion of God, based on His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And whoever honours the sacred rites of God﴾, that is, His religion. It is also said that it means His obligations, which He set down for His servants. ﴿Nor the sacred month﴾, by fighting in it or by postponing it (al-nasi', the intercalation practice of the pagan Arabs). ﴿Nor the offerings﴾, which are what is brought as gifts to the Ka'bah. It is the plural of hadiyyah, like jaday in the plural of jadiyyat al-sarj (the plural pattern of a word used for a saddle-related object). ﴿Nor the garlands﴾, that is, the animals that have garlands from the offerings. It is coupled with the offerings because of its special status, since these are the most noble of the offerings. Or the garlands are the most precious of them. The prohibition against violating them is an intensification of the prohibition against interfering with the offerings. A parallel to this is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Nor reveal their adornment﴾. The word qala'id is the plural of qiladah, which is what the offering is hung with, such as a sandal, the bark of a tree, or other things, so that it is known that it is an offering and is not to be interfered with. ﴿Nor those coming to the Sacred House﴾, intending to visit it. ﴿Seeking bounty from their Lord and His good pleasure﴾, that He may reward them and be pleased with them. The clause is in the position of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to the concealed pronoun in āmmīn (ḥāl, a circumstantial qualifier). It is not a description of it, because the participle is a governing word, and the preferred view is that a described active participle does not govern. Its purpose is to express disapproval of interfering with one whose condition is this, and to draw attention to what prevents such interference. It is also said that the meaning is: they seek from God provision through trade, and good pleasure according to their own belief. It is related that the verse was revealed in the year of the Qadiyyah (the year of the agreement), concerning the pilgrims of Yamamah, when the Muslims intended to confront them, because al-Hutam ibn Shurayh ibn Duba'ah was among them, and he had driven off the livestock of Madinah. On this view the verse is abrogated (mansukhah, naskh being abrogation). It has been read as "tabtaghūna" with the address to the believers. ﴿And when you have come out of the state of ihram, then hunt﴾: this is permission to hunt after the ihram has ended. The intention of permissibility from the command here does not imply that a later command after a prohibition indicates permissibility absolutely. It has been read with a kasrah on the fa', by transferring the vowel of the hamzat al-wasl onto it, and this is very weak. It has been read as "ahlaltum", and it is said: the muhrim halla and ahalla (both mean he came out of ihram). ﴿And let not hatred of a people﴾ lead you to act: it means lay on you or earn for you. ﴿Hatred of a people﴾ is the intensity of their enmity and hostility, and it is a verbal noun (maṣdar) added to the object or to the subject. Ibn 'Amir, Isma'il from Nafi', and Ibn 'Ayyash from 'Asim read it with a sukun on the nun, and it is also a verbal noun like layyān, or an adjective meaning "one who hates a people". The pattern fi'lān is more common in adjectives, like 'aṭshān and sakrān. ﴿That they barred you from the Sacred Mosque﴾: because they barred you from it in the year of al-Hudaybiyyah. Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read it with a kasrah on the hamzah, as a parenthetical conditional clause whose answer is dispensed with, which is "let it not lead you". ﴿To transgress﴾, by retaliation. This is the second object of "let it not lead you", for it takes one object and two objects, like kasaba. Whoever reads "yujrimannakum" with a damma on the ya' makes it the transitive form, through the hamzah, of the verb that takes one object, so that it takes two. ﴿And cooperate in righteousness and piety﴾: through pardon, forbearance, following the command, and turning away from desire. ﴿And do not cooperate in sin and aggression﴾: for the sake of revenge and retaliation. ﴿And fear God; indeed God is severe in punishment﴾, so His retribution is more severe.

﴿Forbidden to you is carrion﴾ explains what is recited to you. Carrion (maytah) is that from which the soul has departed without proper slaughter (tadhkiyah, ritual slaughter). ﴿And blood﴾, meaning flowing blood, as in His words, ﴿or blood poured forth﴾. The people of the Jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance before Islam) used to pour it into intestines and roast them. ﴿And the flesh of swine, and that over which other than God has been invoked﴾, meaning that the voice was raised for other than God when slaughtering it, as when they said, "In the name of al-Lat and al-Uzza." ﴿And the strangled﴾, meaning that which died by strangulation. ﴿And the beaten to death﴾, meaning that which was struck with something like a stick or a stone until it died, from "waqadtuhu" (I struck him) when you strike him.

﴿And the fallen to death﴾, that which fell from a height or into a well and died. ﴿And the gored﴾, that which another animal gored and it died from the goring; the "ta'" in it is for transmission (naql, i.e., it denotes the feminine form of the noun as a transferred noun). ﴿And what the beast of prey has eaten﴾, that of which a beast of prey ate and then it died. This indicates that hunting animals (jawarih al-sayd) which eat from what they have caught are not lawful. ﴿Except what you have slaughtered﴾, except what you reached in its slaughter while there remained a stable life in it from that. It was said that the exception is restricted to what the beast of prey has eaten. Dhakah (slaughter) in the Sharia is the cutting of the windpipe (hulqum) and the gullet (mari’) with a sharp instrument.

﴿And what is sacrificed on the stone altars﴾. Nusub is the singular of ansab, which are stones set up around the House (the Ka'bah), upon which they slaughtered and considered this an act of drawing near (to God). It was said they are idols, and "ala" here has the meaning of "li" (for), or it remains "ala" in its original sense, with the implied construction "and what was slaughtered named upon the idols." It was also said that nusub is a plural and its singular is nisab.

﴿And that you seek decision through the arrows﴾, meaning: and the seeking of decision through the arrows (al-istiqsam bi'l-azlam) was forbidden to you. This is because when they intended an action, they would cast three arrows. On one was written, "My Lord has commanded me," on another, "My Lord has forbidden me," and the third was blank (ghufl). If the command arrow came out, they proceeded with that; if the prohibiting arrow came out, they refrained from it; and if the blank came out, they cast them again a second time. Thus the meaning of istiqsam is seeking knowledge of what has been allotted to them, rather than what has not been allotted to them, by means of the arrows. It was also said: it is the dividing of a slaughtered camel by arrows according to known shares. The singular of azlam is zalam, like jamal, and zulam, like surad.

﴿That is wickedness﴾. The reference is to the istiqsam. Its being wickedness is because it is an entry into the knowledge of the unseen, and misguidance through the belief that this is a path to it, and fabrication against God, glorified and exalted is He, if by "my Lord" God is meant; and ignorance and polytheism if by it an idol is meant, or the forbidden gambling, or the consumption of what was forbidden to them.

﴿Today﴾: it does not refer to a specific day, but intends the present time and the times connected with it that are to come. It was said that it intends the day of its revelation, and it was revealed after the afternoon prayer of Friday, on the Day of Arafah, during the Farewell Pilgrimage (Hajjat al-Wada').

﴿The disbelievers have despaired of your religion﴾, meaning: of its abolition and of your returning from it by permitting these abominations and others, or of their overcoming you in it. So do not fear them that they will prevail over you. ﴿And fear Me﴾, and devote your fear sincerely to Me.

﴿Today I have perfected for you your religion﴾, by granting victory and making it manifest over all other religions; or by stating explicitly the foundations of the beliefs and specifying the principles of the laws and the rules of ijtihad (independent legal reasoning).

﴿And I have completed My favor upon you﴾, by guidance and success; or by the completion of the religion; or by the conquest of Makkah and the demolition of the landmarks of the Jahiliyyah. ﴿And I have approved for you Islam as a religion﴾, meaning I have chosen it for you as a religion from among the religions, and it is the religion with God, and no other.

﴿Whoever is compelled﴾ is connected with the mention of the forbidden things, and what lies between them is a parenthetical clause (i'tiradh) explaining what necessitates avoiding them, namely that consuming them is wickedness, and their prohibition is part of the complete religion, the perfect favor, and the approved Islam. The meaning is: whoever is compelled to consume something of these forbidden things ﴿in a state of severe hunger﴾, meaning famine, ﴿without inclining toward sin﴾, meaning not inclined to it or deviating toward it, by eating it for pleasure or exceeding the limit of the dispensation, as in His words: ﴿neither desiring nor transgressing﴾. ﴿Indeed God is Forgiving and Merciful﴾, He will not hold him accountable for eating it.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 4:

﴿They ask you what has been made lawful for them.﴾ Because the question contains the sense of saying, the verb is followed by a whole clause. The discussion of "what" (mādhā) has already passed. He said "for them" and did not say "for us," as a report of speech, because "they ask you" is in the third-person form, and both ways are permissible in similar expressions. What is asked about is what has been made lawful for them of foods, as if, when what had been forbidden to them was recited to them, they asked about what had been made lawful for them. ﴿Say: Lawful for you are the good things.﴾ These are what sound natural disposition does not find repugnant and from which it does not recoil. From its implication, the things found repulsive by the Arabs are forbidden; or, it is what no text or analogy indicates is forbidden. ﴿And what you have taught from the trained predators.﴾ It is joined to "the good things" if "mā" is taken as a relative pronoun, on the estimate of "and the hunting of what you have taught." If it is taken as a conditional, the clause is conditional and its answer is "then eat." The jawāriḥ (trained predators, lit. "those that seize") are the hunting beasts and birds of prey among their kinds: beasts with four limbs and birds. ﴿Mukallibīn﴾ means training them to hunt. The mukallib (trainer) is one who disciplines the predators and harms them through the hunt, derived from kalb (dog), because the discipline is more and more pronounced in it, or because every predatory beast is called a kalb, based on his saying, upon him be prayer and peace, "O God, set upon him a dog from Your dogs."

Its position is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) from "you have taught," and its benefit is the emphasis on teaching.

﴿You teach them﴾ is a second circumstantial state, or a new independent clause. ﴿From what God has taught you﴾ refers to the stratagems and methods of discipline, for knowledge of them is an inspiration from God, Exalted, or is acquired by reason, which is a gift from Him, glorified and exalted; or, "from what God has taught you" means that you teach them to follow the game upon the release of their master, to be restrained by his restraint, to turn away at his call, and to hold the game for him and not eat from it. ﴿So eat of what they hold for you﴾ means what they have not eaten from, for his saying, upon him be prayer and peace, to ʿAdī ibn Ḥātim: "And if it has eaten from it, do not eat, for it has only held for itself."

Most jurists went to this, and some said: this condition is not required for birds of prey, because training them to this degree is impossible; others said it is not required at all. ﴿And mention the name of God over it﴾: the pronoun refers to "what you have taught," and the meaning is: pronounce God's name over it at its release; or, referring to "what they hold," in the sense of: pronounce God's name over it when you reach its slaughter. ﴿And fear God﴾ regarding His prohibitions. ﴿Indeed God is swift in reckoning﴾, so He will call you to account for what is great and what is small.

The commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on Surah 5, verse 5:

﴿Today the good things have been made lawful for you, and the food of those who were given the Scripture is lawful for you﴾. It covers slaughtered animals and other things. It includes the People of the Book (ahl al-kitab, those who were given earlier scripture), namely the Jews and the Christians. ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with him, made an exception for the Christians of the tribe of Banu Taghlib and said: "They are not upon Christianity; they took from it only the drinking of wine." The Magians (al-majus, Zoroastrians) are not included with them in this ruling, although they are included with them in the matter of being allowed to remain under the jizya (poll tax) arrangement, because of the words of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Treat them as you treat the People of the Book, except that you may not marry their women nor eat their slaughtered animals."

﴿And your food is lawful for them﴾: there is no objection for you to feed them or sell it to them. Had it been forbidden for them, it would not be permissible to do so.

﴿And chaste women from among the believing women﴾: that is, free women, or women of chastity. Specifying them is an exhortation to what is better.

﴿And chaste women from among those who were given the Scripture before you﴾, even if they are from the people of hostile territory (harbiyyat). Ibn ʿAbbas said: the women of hostile territory are not lawful.

﴿When you have given them their wages﴾: their dowries (mahr). Making the lawfulness conditional upon giving them emphasizes its obligation and encourages what is better. It has also been said that the meaning of giving them is committing to them, while they are chaste and virtuous through marriage.

﴿Not as fornicators﴾: not openly committing adultery. ﴿Nor as those who take secret lovers﴾: secretly doing so. The word khidn (secret lover) means a close friend and applies to both male and female.

﴿And whoever disbelieves in the faith, his deeds have become void, and he in the Hereafter will be among the losers﴾: by "faith" he means the laws of Islam, and by "disbelief" he means denying them and refusing them.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (*Anwar al-Tanzil*) on surah 5, verse 6:

﴿O you who believe, when you rise to the prayer﴾, i.e., when you intend to stand for it, like His saying, ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan﴾. He expressed the intention of the act by the act it causes, for brevity and to alert that whoever intends worship should hasten to it, such that the act is never separated from the intention. Or it means: when you intend the prayer, because turning towards a thing and standing up for it is an intention toward it. The apparent meaning of the verse requires wudu' (ablution) for everyone who stands up for prayer, even if he is not in a state of ritual impurity (hadath). The consensus (ijma', the agreement of the scholars) is against this, based on what is reported: that he (ﷺ) prayed the five prayers with one ablution on the day of the Conquest, so ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "You have done something you did not used to do." He said: "I did it deliberately."

It has been said: it is an absolute (muṭlaq) statement intended to be restricted (taqyīd), and the meaning is: when you rise to the prayer in a state of ritual impurity (muḥdithīn). It has been said: the command in it is for recommendation (nadb). It has been said: this was at the beginning of the matter and then it was abrogated (naskh, the cancellation of a ruling by later revelation), but this is weak, due to his saying (ﷺ): "Al-Ma'idah is among the last of the Qur'an to be revealed, so make lawful its lawful things and make unlawful its unlawful things."

﴿So wash your faces﴾: let the water pass over them. There is no need for rubbing (dalk), contrary to Malik.

﴿And your hands up to the elbows﴾. The majority hold that the two elbows enter into what is washed. For this reason it has been said: "ilā" here means "maʿa" (with), like His saying, ﴿and He will add strength to your strength﴾. Or it is connected to an omitted element, its estimated sense being: "and your hands, extended up to the elbows." If this were the case, the restrictive sense would not remain, nor would its mention have any additional benefit, since the absolute term "hand" includes them.

It has been said: "ilā" indicates the limit (ghāyah) absolutely, but as for whether it enters into the ruling or exits from it, it has no indication of this, and it is known only from outside the verse, which is not in the verse. The hands cover it, so it was ruled that it enters, out of caution (iḥtiyāṭ). It has been said: "ilā" here, insofar as it indicates a limit, requires its exclusion, otherwise it would not be a limit, as in His saying, ﴿then [grant him] postponement until a time of ease﴾ and His saying, ﴿then complete the fast until the night﴾. However, since the limit is not distinguished here from the thing limited, its inclusion is required out of caution.

﴿And wipe over your heads﴾: the "bāʾ" (preposition) is extra (zā'idah). It has been said it is for partialness (tab'īḍ), for it is what distinguishes between your saying "I wiped the handkerchief" and "I wiped with the handkerchief." Its explanation is that it can be said that it indicates the implication of the verb with the meaning of adhesion (ilṣāq), as if it were said: "and make the wiping adhere to your heads." That does not require covering the whole, unlike what would be if it were said: "and wipe your heads," for that would be like His saying: "So wash your faces and your..." (p-117)

If it were said: "wipe your heads," it would be like His saying, "wash your faces." The scholars differed about the amount that is obligatory. Al-Shafiʿi, may Allah be pleased with him, held that it is the least amount to which the name applies, taking the certain. Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, held that it is wiping a quarter of the head, because he (ﷺ) wiped over his forelock (nāṣiyah), which is close to a quarter. Malik, may Allah be pleased with him, held that it is wiping all of it, taking the cautious course.

﴿And your feet up to the ankles﴾. Nafiʿ, Ibn ʿAmir, Hafs, al-Kisaʾi and Yaʿqub put it in the accusative (naṣb), coordinating it with "your faces." This is supported by the widespread Sunnah, the practice of the Companions, the statement of most of the imams, and the fact that limiting (taḥdīd) applies, since wiping has not been limited.

The rest read it in the genitive (jarr) by attraction to the adjacent word (jiwār). Its parallel is abundant in the Qur'an and in poetry, like His saying, ﴿the punishment of a painful day﴾, and ﴿and [with] wide-eyed maidens﴾, read with the genitive in the recitation of Hamzah and al-Kisaʾi, and the saying "juḥr ḍabb khirib" (the hole of a ruined lizard). The grammarians have a chapter on this. Its benefit is to alert that one should be moderate in pouring water over them and wash them in a manner close to wiping, and in separating it from its two counterparts is an indication of the obligation of the sequence (tartīb). It was also read with the nominative (raf'), as "wa-arjulukum" (and your feet) being washed (maghsūlah).

﴿And if you are in a state of janabah, then purify yourselves﴾: then wash your whole body.

﴿And if you are ill or on a journey, or one of you comes from the place of relieving oneself, or you have touched women, and you find no water, then take clean earth and wipe your faces and hands with it﴾: its explanation has preceded. Perhaps its repetition is so that the discourse on the types of purification is connected.

﴿Allah does not intend to place upon you any difficulty﴾: i.e., He does not intend the command of purification for prayer, or the command of tayammum, to be a constraint upon you. ﴿But He intends to purify you﴾: to cleanse you, or to purify you from sins, for ablution is an expiation of sins, or to purify you with dust when purification by water is unavailable to you. So the object of "yurīdu" in both places is omitted, and the "lām" is for causation. It has been said the "lām" is extra, and the meaning is: Allah does not intend to place upon you any difficulty, so that He does not grant you leniency in tayammum; but He intends that He purify you. This is weak, because "an" (that) is not estimated after the extra element.

﴿And that He may complete His favor upon you﴾: so that He may complete, by His law, what is a means of purifying your bodies and expiating your sins, His favor upon you in religion; or so that He may complete, by His concessions, His bounty upon you through His firm commands. ﴿So that you may be grateful﴾ for His favor.

The verse includes seven matters, all of them in pairs: two purifications, a basic one and a substitute (badal); the basic one is of two kinds, comprehensive (mustawʿib) and non-comprehensive; the non-comprehensive, in terms of the action, is washing and wiping, and in terms of the place, is limited and non-limited; and their instrument is liquid and solid; and what necessitates them is minor ritual impurity (ḥadath aṣghar) and major ritual impurity (ḥadath akbar); and what permits turning to the substitute is illness or travel; and what is promised upon them is the purification from sins and the completion of favor.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 7:

﴿And remember the favour of Allah upon you﴾ — that is, Islam — so that it reminds you of the Benefactor (al-Mun'im) and makes you eager to be grateful to Him. ﴿And His covenant with which He bound you when you said, "We hear and we obey"﴾ — meaning the covenant which He took from the Muslims when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) pledged them to hearing and obeying in hardship and ease, in what is pleasant and what is disliked; or His covenant on the night of al-'Aqabah, or the Pledge of al-Ridwan. ﴿And fear Allah﴾ — regarding forgetting His favour and breaking His covenant. ﴿Indeed, Allah is Knower of what is within the breasts﴾ — that is, of their hidden matters, so He will recompense you for them, in addition to your manifest deeds.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 8:

﴿O you who have believed, be persistently standing firm for Allah, witnesses in justice, and do not let the hatred of a people prevent you from being just.﴾ He construed it with ʿalā (on/against) because it includes the meaning of "bearing" (*tadmīn*, the implicit inclusion of one verb's meaning in another). The meaning is: let not the intensity of your hatred for the polytheists drive you to abandon justice toward them, so that you transgress against them by committing what is not permitted, such as mutilation, slander, killing women and children, and breaking covenants, seeking to satisfy what is in your hearts. ﴿Be just; that is nearer to righteousness.﴾ That is, justice is nearer to piety. He expressly commanded them to be just and explained that it is in the position of piety, after forbidding them from injustice and explaining that injustice is the demand of desire. If this is the case for justice toward the disbelievers, then what do you think of justice toward the believers? ﴿And fear Allah. Indeed, Allah is Acquainted with what you do.﴾ So He will recompense you for it. The repetition of this ruling is either because the occasions differ, as it has been said that the first was revealed concerning the polytheists and this one concerning the Jews, or for the sake of greater emphasis on justice and in exaggerating the extinguishing of the blaze of anger. (p-118)

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verses 9–10:

﴿God has promised those who believe and do righteous deeds: for them is forgiveness and a great reward.﴾ The second of the two objects of the verb waʿada (promised) has been omitted, being dispensed with by His saying "for them is forgiveness," which is a resumptive clause (istiʾnaf) that explains it. It has also been said that the clause occupies the position of the object, since promising (waʿd) is a kind of speech, and it is as if He said: "He promised them this statement."

﴿And those who disbelieve and deny Our signs, they are the companions of the Blazing Fire.﴾ This is among His customary practices, glorified is He, that He follows the condition of one of the two groups with the condition of the other, in fulfilment of the right of the call (to faith), and in it there is an added promise to the believers and a consoling of their hearts.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verses 9–10:

﴿God has promised those who believe and do righteous deeds: for them is forgiveness and a great reward.﴾ The second of the two objects of the verb waʿada (promised) has been omitted, being dispensed with by His saying "for them is forgiveness," which is a resumptive clause (istiʾnaf) that explains it. It has also been said that the clause occupies the position of the object, since promising (waʿd) is a kind of speech, and it is as if He said: "He promised them this statement."

﴿And those who disbelieve and deny Our signs, they are the companions of the Blazing Fire.﴾ This is among His customary practices, glorified is He, that He follows the condition of one of the two groups with the condition of the other, in fulfilment of the right of the call (to faith), and in it there is an added promise to the believers and a consoling of their hearts.

**"O you who believe, remember the favor of Allah upon you"** [Qur'an 5:11]. It was narrated that "the polytheists saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his Companions at ʿUsfān. They stood up together for the noon prayer, and when they had prayed they regretted that they had not fallen upon them while they were standing for the afternoon prayer and intended to attack them then. So Allah turned back their scheme by sending down upon them the prayer of fear (ṣalāt al-khawf)."

The verse refers to that. It was also said that it refers to what was narrated: "He (peace and blessings be upon him) went to Qurayza, accompanied by the four caliphs, to ask them for a loan for the blood-money (diya) of two Muslims whom ʿAmr ibn Umayya al-Ḍamrī had killed, thinking they were polytheists. They said, 'Yes, O Abu al-Qasim, sit down until we feed you and lend to you.' They seated him and intended to kill him. ʿAmr ibn Jiḥāsh went to a large millstone to drop it on him, but Allah held back his hand. Then Gabriel came down and informed him, and he went out."

It was also said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stopped at a place and hung his sword on a tree, and the people dispersed from him. A Bedouin came, drew his sword and said, 'Who will protect you from me?' He said, 'Allah!' Gabriel then knocked the sword from his hand. The Messenger (ﷺ) took it and said, 'Who will protect you from me?' He said, 'No one. I testify that there is no god but Allah, and I testify that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah.' Then the verse was revealed."

**"When a people determined to stretch out their hands against you"** [Qur'an 5:11], with killing and destruction. It is said *basaṭa ilayhi yadahu* when one attacks him, and *basaṭa ilayhi lisānahu* when one insults him.

**"But He withheld their hands from you"** [Qur'an 5:11], meaning He restrained them from reaching you and turned their harm away from you.

**"And fear Allah; and upon Allah let the believers rely"** [Qur'an 5:11], for He is the One sufficient for bringing about good and warding off evil.

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 12:**

﴿And Allah had certainly taken the covenant of the Children of Israel, and We raised among them twelve chieftains﴾ (*nuqaba'*, sing. *naqib*): a witness from each tribe (*sibt*) who would investigate and examine the condition of his people. Or (they were) guarantors (*kafil*) who would vouch for them regarding their fulfilment of what they had been commanded.

It is narrated that when the Children of Israel had finished with Pharaoh and settled in Egypt, Allah, glorified and exalted is He, commanded them to set out for Uraiha (Jericho), in the land of Syria. It was inhabited by the tyrannical Canaanites (*al-Kan'aniyyun*). He said: "Indeed, I have decreed it for you as a home and a dwelling place, so go forth to it and fight those who are in it, for indeed I am your helper." Moses, peace be upon him, was commanded to take from each tribe a guarantor over them for their fulfilment of what they had been commanded. So he took the covenant from them, chose the chieftains from among them, and set out with them. When he drew near the land of Canaan, he sent the chieftains to spy out the news, and he forbade them to inform their people. They saw enormous bodies and great might, so they became afraid and returned, informed their people, and broke the covenant, except for Kaleb ibn Yufuna (Caleb son of Jephunneh) of the tribe of Yahudha (Judah), and Yusha' ibn Nun (Joshua son of Nun) of the tribe of Ifra'im ibn Yusuf (Ephraim, son of Joseph). (p-119)

﴿And Allah said: "Indeed I am with you"﴾ in support, ﴿"if you establish the prayer, give the zakat, believe in My messengers and honour them"﴾. That is, you help them and strengthen them. Its root meaning is to defend, and from it comes *ta'zir* (honouring/strengthening). ﴿"And you lend Allah a goodly loan"﴾ by spending in the way of good, and *qard* (loan) may be understood as a verbal noun or as a passive object (i.e., that which is lent). ﴿"I will surely remove from you your misdeeds"﴾: this is the answer to the oath (*jawab al-qasam*), indicated by the *lam* in *la'in* (the particle of oath), and it stands in place of the answer to the condition (*jawab al-shart*). ﴿"And I will surely admit you into gardens beneath which rivers flow. Then whoever disbelieves after that"﴾ after this emphasised condition, upon which the great promise is contingent, ﴿"among you, has indeed strayed from the right way"﴾, a straying with no doubt in it and no excuse accompanying it, unlike one who disbelieved before that, for it is possible that he had some doubt and could imagine for himself an excuse.

**Al-Baydawi's commentary (Anwar al-Tanzil) on Surah 5, verse 13:**

﴿So for their breaking of their covenant, We cursed them﴾: We expelled them from Our mercy, or We transformed them (into apes and swine), or We imposed on them the jizya (the poll tax levied on non-Muslim subjects). ﴿And We made their hearts hard﴾: they are not affected by the signs (āyāt) and warnings (nudhur). Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read «qasiyyatan», which is either an intensive form of qāsiyah (hard), or means "bad," from the saying "dirham qasiyy" when it is adulterated. This also derives from qaswah (hardness), since an adulterated coin has dryness and firmness. It was also read «qisiyyatan», with the qāf made to follow the kasra of the sīn. ﴿They distort words from their places﴾: this is a resumptive sentence (isti'nāf) explaining the hardness of their hearts, since there is no greater hardness than altering the speech of God, glorified and exalted, and fabricating against Him. It is permissible for it to be a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) referring to the object of "laʿannāhum" (We cursed them), not to "qulūb" (hearts), since the latter has no pronoun referring back to it in this clause. ﴿And they forgot a portion﴾: they abandoned a full share ﴿of what they were reminded of﴾, from the Torah, or from following Muhammad (ﷺ). The meaning is that they distorted the Torah and abandoned their share of what was revealed to them, so they did not attain it. It is also said that the meaning is that they distorted it, so that some of it slipped from their memory as a consequence of this, because it was reported that Ibn Mas'ud said: "A person may forget some knowledge through sin," and he recited this verse.

﴿And you will not cease to discover treachery from them﴾: treachery from them, or a treacherous group, or a treacherous person, and the tā' (in khā'inah) is for intensification. The meaning is that treachery and betrayal are their habit and the habit of their predecessors, and you will continue to see this from them. ﴿Except a few of them﴾: those who did not betray, and they are the ones among them who believed. It is also said that it is an exception from His saying: "and We made their hearts hard." ﴿So pardon them and overlook﴾: if they repent and believe, or if they make a covenant and commit to paying the jizya. It is said: this is an unrestricted command that was abrogated (nusikha, i.e., naskh, abrogation) by the verse of the sword. ﴿Indeed, God loves the good-doers﴾: this is a reason given for the command to forgive, and an exhortation to it, and an alert that pardoning a treacherous disbeliever is an act of goodness, let alone pardoning others.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 14:

﴿And among those who say, "We are Christians," We took their covenant﴾ That is: and We took the covenant of the Christians just as We took it from those before them. It has also been said that its construction is: "And among those who say, 'We are Christians,' is a people We took [a covenant from]." He said "who say, 'We are Christians'" to indicate that they named themselves thus, claiming to be the helpers of God, glorified and exalted is He. ﴿But they forgot a portion of what they were reminded of, so We stirred up﴾ That is, We attached [enmity]; from "ghariya bi-l-shay'" (he clung to the thing) when it adhered to him. ﴿enmity and hatred among them until the Day of Resurrection.﴾ Among the sects of the Christians, namely the Nestorians, the Jacobites and the Melkites; or between them and the Jews. ﴿And God will soon inform them of what they used to do.﴾ With reward and punishment.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 15:

﴿O People of the Scripture﴾ meaning the Jews and the Christians. He used the singular "Scripture" (al-Kitab) because it refers to the category (li-l-jins) in general. ﴿There has certainly come to you Our Messenger, making clear to you much of what you used to conceal of the Scripture﴾ (p-120) such as the description of Muhammad (ﷺ), the verse of stoning (ayat al-rajm) in the Torah, and the good tidings of Jesus, upon him be peace, concerning Ahmad (ﷺ) in the Gospel. ﴿And he pardons much﴾ of what you conceal: he does not disclose it when no religious matter necessitates it; or it means he pardons many of you, so he does not hold you to account for your sin. ﴿There has certainly come to you from Allah a light and a clear Book﴾ meaning the Qur'an, for it is what uncovers the darkness of doubt and misguidance, and the Book that is manifest in its inimitability (i'jaz). It has also been said that by the light is meant Muhammad (ﷺ).

﴿Yahdi bihi Allah﴾ (God guides by it). He used the singular pronoun because the referent of both is one, or because they are like a single thing in ruling.

﴿Man ittaba'a ridwanahu﴾ (whoever follows His good pleasure): whoever follows His pleasure by faith among them.

﴿Subula as-salam﴾ (paths of peace): the ways of safety from punishment, or the paths of God.

﴿Wa yukhrijuhum mina adh-dhulumati ila an-nur﴾ (and brings them out of darknesses into light): from the kinds of disbelief to Islam.

﴿Bi idhnihi﴾ (by His permission): by His will, or His enabling success.

﴿Wa yahdihim ila sirat mustaqim﴾ (and guides them to a straight path): a path that is the nearest of paths to God, glorified and exalted be He, and that inevitably leads to Him.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 17:

﴿Certainly they have disbelieved who say, "Indeed, Allah is the Messiah, son of Mary."﴾ They are those among them who spoke of (al-ittihad) (incarnation, the union of God with a human being). It is said that none of them explicitly stated this, but when they claimed that there is divinity (lahut) in him, and said "There is no god but Allah, He is One," it followed for them that He is the Messiah. So He attributed to them the necessary implication of their statement, as a clarification of their ignorance and an exposure of their belief.

﴿Say: "Then who has any power against Allah at all"﴾ i.e., who can prevent any thing from His power and His will?

﴿if He had intended to destroy the Messiah﴾ i.e., Jesus, ﴿son of Mary, and his mother and everyone on earth entirely?﴾ He argued with this against the corruption of their minds. Its formulation is: the Messiah is subject to power, overpowered, capable of perishing like all contingent beings, and whoever is so is far removed from divinity.

﴿And to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is between them. He creates what He wills, and Allah is over all things competent.﴾ This removes the doubt that had been presented to them concerning His matter. The meaning is that He, glorified and exalted be He, is absolutely powerful: He creates without any origin, as He created the heavens and the earth, and from an origin, as in the creation of what is between them. So He originates from an origin that is not of its kind, like Adam and many animals; and from an origin of its own kind, either from a male alone, as He created Eve, or from a female alone, as with Jesus, or from both, as with the rest of mankind.

﴿And the Jews and the Christians said, "We are the sons of God and His beloved."﴾ (They are) the followers of His two sons, Uzayr and the Messiah, just as it was said of the followers of Ibn al-Zubayr that they were the Khubaybun, or the Muqarrabun (those brought near) to Him, with the nearness of children to their father. A fuller explanation of similar matters has already been given in Surah Al 'Imran.

﴿Say: "Then why does He punish you for your sins?"﴾ That is: if what you claim is true, then why does He punish you for your sins? For whoever holds this rank does not do what would require his punishment. He has indeed punished you in this world by killing, captivity and transformation, and you have acknowledged that He will punish you with the Fire for a number of counted days.

﴿Rather, you are human beings among those He has created.﴾ Among those whom God Most High has created. ﴿He forgives whom He wills﴾ and they are those who believe in Him and His messengers. ﴿And He punishes whom He wills﴾ and they are those who disbelieve. The meaning is that He treats you as He treats the rest of mankind; you have no distinction with Him. ﴿And to God belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and what is between them﴾ all of them alike in being His creation and His possession. ﴿And to Him is the final return﴾ so He will recompense the doer of good for his good and the doer of evil for his evil.

(p-121) "O People of the Scripture, there has certainly come to you Our Messenger, making clear to you" — that is, (making clear) the religion; the object is omitted because it is evident. Or (the object is) "what you were concealing," and it is omitted because its mention has preceded. It is also permissible not to posit an object, with the meaning of "giving you the clarification." The clause is then in the position of a circumstantial (ḥāl): "there has come to you Our Messenger, making clear to you."

"After a lapse (fatrah) of messengers" — this is connected to "has come to you": that is, he came at a time of cessation of sending and a break in revelation. Or "making clear" is a circumstantial clause relating to the pronoun in it.

"Lest you should say, 'There came to us no bearer of good news and no warner.'" — (this was) out of aversion that you would say that and make it an excuse.

"Indeed, there has come to you a bearer of good news and a warner." — this is connected to an omitted element, meaning: do not make excuse with "there came to us," for there has come to you.

"And Allah is over all things Competent." — He is capable of sending messengers in succession, as He did between Moses and Jesus, peace be upon them both, for between them were one thousand seven hundred years and one thousand prophets; and of sending (messengers) after a lapse, as He did between Jesus and Muhammad, peace be upon them both: between them were six hundred or five hundred and sixty-nine years, and four prophets, three of the Children of Israel and one of the Arabs, Khalid ibn Sinan al-'Absi. In the verse there is a favour upon them, in that He sent to them when the traces of revelation had been effaced and they were most in need of it.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 20:

﴿And when Musa said to his people: "O my people, remember the favour of Allah upon you when He appointed prophets among you﴾ and guided you and honoured you through them, and He did not send to any nation what He sent to the Children of Israel of prophets. ﴿And made you kings﴾, i.e., and made from among you or in you [kings]. Kings multiplied among them, just as prophets multiplied after Fir'awn (Pharaoh), to the extent that they killed Yahya (John) and intended to kill Isa (Jesus). It was also said: because they had been enslaved in the hands of the Copts, Allah rescued them and made them masters of their own selves and their affairs, and so He called them kings. ﴿And gave you what He had not given to anyone else among the worlds﴾, namely the splitting of the sea, the shading of the clouds, the sending down of manna and quails, and the like of what Allah gave them. It was also said that what is meant by "the worlds" is the worlds of their own times.

﴿O my people, enter the holy land﴾, the land of Bayt al-Maqdis. It was called so because it was the abode (qarar) of the prophets, upon them be blessings and peace, and the dwelling place of the believers. It is said: it is Mount Sinai (al-Tur) and what surrounds it. It is said: Damascus, Palestine, and part of Jordan. It is said: al-Sham.

﴿which God has prescribed for you﴾: He allotted it to you, or it was written in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh) that it would be a dwelling for you. But if you believe and obey, (this applies), in reference to His saying to them after they disobeyed, then it is forbidden to them.

﴿And do not turn back on your heels﴾: do not return retreating out of fear of the tyrants. It is said: when they heard their condition from the nuqaba' (chiefs of the tribes), they wept and said: "Would that we had died in Egypt! Come, let us appoint a leader who will turn us back to Egypt." Or it means: do not turn back from your religion through disobedience and lack of trust in God, glorified and exalted be He. ﴿Then you will turn back as losers﴾, losing the reward of both abodes. In fatanqalibu it is permissible to read the verb in the jussive (jazm) by conjunction (atf), and in the accusative (nasb) as an answer (jawab) to the prior imperative.

﴿They said: O Musa, indeed in it is a people of tyrants﴾, dominant (mutaghallibin), whose opposition cannot be achieved. Jabbar is on the pattern fa''al, from jabarahu 'ala al-amr, meaning ajbarahu, that is, one who compels people to what he wants. ﴿And indeed we will never enter it until they leave it; so if they leave it, then indeed we will enter﴾, since we have no strength against them.

(p-122)

[Two men said]: Kaleb and Yusha'. [Among those who fear]: i.e., who fear Allah, glorified and exalted, and are mindful of Him. It is said that the two men were from among the giants (al-jababira) who had embraced Islam and went to Musa, peace be upon him. According to this view, the *waw* in *al-ladhina* refers to the Children of Israel, and the returning pronoun in the relative clause is omitted, meaning "from those whom the Children of Israel fear." What supports this is that it was recited as *alladhina yukhafun* with a *damma* on the *yā'*, meaning "those who cause fear" (al-mukhawwifin). According to the first meaning, this is from *al-ikhafah* (causing fear), i.e., "from among those who warn of Allah, mighty and majestic, by reminding them, or whom the threat of punishment frightens." ﴿Allah has bestowed His favor upon them both﴾ with faith and steadfastness. This is a second attribute of "two men," or it is a parenthetical clause. ﴿Enter upon them through the gate﴾: the gate of their town, i.e., surprise them, press upon them in the narrow passage, and prevent them from going out into the open country. ﴿For when you enter it, you will surely be victorious﴾: because it is difficult to charge against them in narrow places due to the great size of their bodies, and because they are bodies without hearts. It is also possible that their knowledge of this came from Musa's report, peace be upon him, and his saying: ﴿Allah has decreed for you﴾, or from what they knew of Allah's custom, glorified and exalted, in supporting His messengers, and what they had witnessed of His handiwork for Musa, peace be upon him, in subduing his enemies. ﴿And upon Allah rely, if you are believers﴾: i.e., believers in Him and affirmers of His promise.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verses 24–25:

﴿They said, "O Musa, indeed we will never enter it, ever, as long as they remain within it."﴾ They negated their entry with emphasis (al-ta'kid) and perpetuity (al-ta'bid). The phrase ﴿as long as they remain within it﴾ is a substitution (badal) for "ever," a badal al-ba'd (partial substitution). ﴿So go, you and your Lord, and fight. Indeed, we will remain seated here.﴾ They said this out of contempt for Allah and His Messenger and disregard for both of them. It was also said that its implied meaning is: "Go, you and your Lord, and He will help you."

﴿He said, "My Lord, I have no control except over myself and my brother."﴾ He said this as a complaint of his distress and grief to Allah, glorified and exalted be He, because his people had opposed him and he had despaired of them, and no companion remained with him whom he trusted except Harun, peace be upon him. As for the two men mentioned, although they agreed with him, he did not trust them, because of what he had suffered from the inconstancy of his people. It is also permissible that "my brother" refers to whoever is a brother to me in religion, so that the two men would be included. The word "brother" may be read in the accusative, as a conjunction (atf) upon "myself," or upon the noun of inna; its nominative reading is a conjunction upon the pronoun in "I have no control," or upon the position (mahall) of inna and its noun; and its genitive reading, according to the Kufans, is a conjunction upon the pronoun in "myself." ﴿So separate us from the defiantly disobedient people.﴾ That is, by judging in our favor what we deserve and judging against them what they deserve, or by distancing between us and them and freeing us from their company.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 26:

﴿He said: "Indeed, it is"﴾ — that is, the Holy Land. ﴿forbidden to them﴾ — they will neither enter it nor possess it, because of their disobedience.

﴿for forty years they will wander in the land﴾ — The governing element of the time phrase ("forty years") may be "forbidden." In that case the prohibition is temporary, not perpetual, and it does not contradict the apparent sense of His words ﴿which Allah has decreed for you﴾. This is supported by what is related: that Musa, upon him be peace, traveled after him with those of the Children of Israel who remained, conquered Ariha (Jericho), stayed there for as long as Allah willed, and then died.

It is also said: he died during the wandering (al-tih). When he was near death, he informed them that Yusha' (Joshua) would be a prophet after him and that Allah, glorified and exalted, had commanded him to fight the tyrants (al-jababira). Yusha' then led them, killed the tyrants, and all of Syria (al-Sham) became the possession of the Children of Israel.

Or the governing element is "they will wander," meaning they will travel in it, bewildered, unable to see a path, in which case the prohibition is absolute. It has been said that none of those who said, "Indeed, we will never enter it," entered the Holy Land; rather, they perished in the wandering, and it was their children who fought the tyrants.

It is related that they remained forty years within a radius of six farsakh, traveling from morning until evening, and then found themselves in the same place they had departed from. The cloud shaded them from the sun, and a pillar of light would rise at night and illuminate for them. Their food was manna and quail, and their water came from the stone they carried. Most scholars hold that Musa and Harun were with them in the wandering, though this was a comfort to them both and an increase in their rank, and a punishment for the people. Both of them died during it: Harun died, and Musa died a year after him. Then Yusha' entered Ariha after three months. The chieftains (al-nuqaba') died during it suddenly, except Caleb (Kalib) and Yusha'.

﴿So do not grieve over the defiantly disobedient people﴾ — Musa, upon him be peace, was addressed with this when he regretted having invoked curses against them, and it was made clear that they deserved this because of their wickedness.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verses 27–28:

﴿Recite to them the story of the two sons of Adam⁠﴾ — Qabil and Habil. God, glorified and exalted be He, revealed to Adam that he should marry each of them to the twin of the other. Qabil became angry about this because his twin was more beautiful. So Adam said to them both: "Offer a sacrifice (qurban), and whichever of you is accepted shall marry her." The sacrifice of Habil was accepted, in that a fire descended and consumed it, and Qabil's anger increased, and he did what he did. It is also said that the two were not the sons of Adam by his loins, but two men from the Children of Israel, and for this reason He said: ﴿We prescribed for the Children of Israel⁠﴾. "With truth" (bil-haqq) is an adjective of a deleted verbal noun, meaning a recitation accompanied by truth; or it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "recite"; or from "story", meaning accompanied by sincerity, in agreement with what is in the books of the earlier peoples. ﴿When they both offered a sacrifice⁠﴾ is a temporal clause (zarf) related to "story", or a circumstantial clause from it, or a substitute (badal) with a deleted modifier, meaning: recite to them the story of them both, the story of that time. The qurban (sacrifice) is the name of what one draws near to God, glorified and exalted be He, by, whether a slaughtered animal or otherwise, just as al-hulwan (gift) is the name of what one is adorned with, i.e., given. Originally it is a verbal noun, and for this reason it is not made dual. It is also said its implied meaning is: when each of them offered a sacrifice. It is said that Qabil was a farmer and offered the worst grain he had, and Habil was a herder and offered a fat camel. ﴿So it was accepted from one of them, and was not accepted from the other⁠﴾, because he (the other) was angry at the judgment of God, glorified and exalted be He, did not make his intention sincere in his offering, and aimed at the basest of what he had. ﴿He said: "I will surely kill you"⁠﴾ — he threatened him with killing, out of extreme envy of him because of the acceptance of his sacrifice, and for that reason. ﴿He said: "God only accepts from the God-fearing"⁠﴾ — in reply to him, i.e., you were brought to this by your own self through abandoning God-consciousness, not from my side, so why would you kill me? In this is an indication that the envious person should see his deprivation as stemming from his own shortcoming, and should strive to acquire what made the envied one fortunate, not to remove his blessing, for that harms him and does not benefit him; and that obedience is accepted only from a believer who is God-fearing.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verses 27–28:

It is also said that the two were not the sons of Adam by his loins, but two men from the Children of Israel, and for this reason He said: ﴿We prescribed for the Children of Israel⁠﴾. "With truth" (bil-haqq) is an adjective of a deleted verbal noun, meaning a recitation accompanied by truth; or it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in "recite"; or from "story", meaning accompanied by sincerity, in agreement with what is in the books of the earlier peoples. ﴿When they both offered a sacrifice⁠﴾ is a temporal clause (zarf) related to "story", or a circumstantial clause from it, or a substitute (badal) with a deleted modifier, meaning: recite to them the story of them both, the story of that time. Originally it is a verbal noun, and for this reason it is not made dual. It is also said its implied meaning is: when each of them offered a sacrifice. Commentary of al-Baydawi (*Anwar al-Tanzil*) on surah 5, verses 29–30:

﴿I intend that you should bear my sin and your own sin, and so be among the companions of the Fire. That is the recompense of the wrongdoers.﴾ This is a second reason for refraining from opposing and resisting. The meaning is: I only submit to you, wanting that you bear my sin should I stretch out my hand to you, and your sin by your stretching your hand to me. Its like is the statement of the two, "The one who reviles first, the sin is upon him, as long as the wronged one does not transgress." It has been said that the meaning of "with my sin" is with the sin of my killing, and "with your sin" is the sin on account of which your offering was not accepted. Both are in the position of a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), meaning you return laden with both sins, carrying them. Perhaps he did not intend the disobedience of his brother and his wretchedness. Rather, his aim in this speech is that, if that is inevitably going to happen, then I want it to be for you and not for me. (p-124)

So the intended meaning is, in essence, that the sin should not be his, not that it should belong to his brother. It is also permissible for "sin" to mean its punishment, and wishing punishment upon the disobedient is permissible.

﴿So his soul facilitated for him the killing of his brother.﴾ That is, it made it easy for him and expanded it for him, from *ṭāʿa lahu al-marta'* ("the pasture became accommodating for him") when it became wide. It is also read as *fa-ṭāwaʿat* (the soul "complied"), with the subject being the soul, in the sense of *fa-ʿalat* ("it did"). Alternatively, the killing of his brother is as if it called her to undertake it, and she complied with it. The *lahu* (for him) is for added connection, like your saying, "I guarded Zayd's property for him" (*ḥafiẓtu li-Zaydin mālahu*). ﴿So he killed him, and became among the losers.﴾ That is, in religion and in worldly life, for he remained, for the duration of his life, banished and grieving. It has been said that Hābīl was killed at the age of twenty, at the Ḥirāʾ ridge (*ʿAqabat Ḥirāʾ*). It has also been said that it was in Basra, at the site of the Great Mosque (*al-Masjid al-Aʿẓam*).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 31:

﴿So God sent a raven scratching in the earth, to show him how to conceal his brother's corpse.﴾ It is related that when he killed him, he was bewildered about what to do with him, since he was the first dead person among the children of Adam. So God sent two ravens, which fought, and one of them killed the other. Then it dug a grave for it with its beak and feet, and cast it into the pit. The pronoun in *liyurayahu* (لِيُرِيَهُ, "to show him") refers either to God, glorified and exalted, or to the raven. *Kayfa* (كَيْفَ, "how") is a circumstantial clause (*hal*, حال) relating to the pronoun in *yuwari* (يُوارِي, "conceal"), and the clause is the second of the two objects of *yuriya* (يُرِيَ, "show"). By "his brother's corpse" (*sawata akhihi*, سَوْءَةَ أخِيهِ) is meant his dead body, since it is something repugnant to be seen. ﴿He said, "Woe is me!"﴾ This is an expression of distress and grief, and the *alif* in *waylata* (ويْلَتا) is a substitute for the first-person *ya'* (ياء المتكلم, the "ya" of the speaker). The meaning is: "O my woe, come, for this is your time." *Al-Wayl* and *al-Waylah* (الوَيْلُ والوَيْلَةُ) mean ruin. ﴿Have I been unable to be like this raven and conceal my brother's corpse?﴾ That is, I am not guided to the like of what it was guided to. His saying *fa-uwariya* (فَأُوارِيَ, "and conceal") is conjoined (*ma'tuf*, عُطِفَ) upon *akuna* (أكُونَ, "to be"), and it is not the answer to the interrogative, since the meaning here is not "if I were unable, I would have concealed," and it has been read with a sukun (سُكُونِ) as *fa-ana uwari* (فَأنا أُوارِي, "so I conceal"), or as the sukun of the accusative for lightness (تَخْفِيفًا). ﴿So he became one of the regretful.﴾ Regretful for killing him, because of what he endured of bewilderment about his affair, and of carrying him on his back for a year or more, as it is said, and of his being a student of the raven, the blackening of his complexion, and his parents' disavowal of him. For it is related that when he killed him, his body turned black, so Adam asked him about his brother, and he said, "I was not a guardian over him." Adam said, "Rather, you killed him, and that is why your body has turned black." He disowned him. He remained after that for a hundred years without laughing, and without attaining success in what he had done for its sake.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 32:

﴿Because of that We decreed for the Children of Israel﴾ that is, by reason of it We enjoined upon them. Ajl, originally, is a verbal noun of ajala sharran, meaning "he committed evil," and it came to be used to express the cause of offences, as in the saying, "min jarraka fa'altuhu" (I did it because of you), meaning "min an jarartuhu," that is, "because I committed it against you." Then its usage was broadened so that it was employed for every kind of causation. Min here is for the beginning (ibtida'iyya), connected to katabna (We decreed), meaning that the beginning and origin of the decree was because of that. ﴿That whoever kills a soul, unless for a soul, or for corruption in the land﴾ that is, without a killing that necessitates retaliation (qisas). ﴿Or for corruption in the land﴾ or without corruption in it, such as shirk (polytheism) or highway robbery.

﴿It is as if he had slain all mankind﴾ either because he has violated the sanctity of blood, established killing as a precedent, and emboldened people against it; or because the killing of one and the killing of all are equal in drawing upon oneself the wrath of Allah, glorified and exalted be He, and a mighty punishment. ﴿And whoever gives life to it, it is as if he had given life to all mankind﴾ that is, whoever causes its life to continue by pardoning, or by preventing it from being killed, or by rescuing it from some causes of destruction, it is as if he had done that for all mankind. The purpose of this is to magnify the killing of a soul and the preservation of its life in hearts, as a deterrent from attacking it and as an encouragement to protect it.

﴿And indeed Our messengers came to them with clear proofs; then indeed many of them, after that, in the land, are transgressors﴾ that is, after We had prescribed for them this great severity because of the likes of that crime, and sent to them the messengers with clear signs, as confirmation of the command and renewal of the covenant so that they would keep away from it, many of them nonetheless commit excess in the land by killing and do not care about it. With this, the narrative is connected to what preceded it. Israf (excess) means going beyond the limit of moderation in a matter.(p-125)

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 33:

﴿Indeed, the recompense of those who wage war against Allah and His Messenger﴾ means: those who wage war against their allies, who are the Muslims; He made waging war against them as waging war against Them, as a glorification. The root of ḥarb (war) is plunder (al-salb), and what is meant by it here is highway robbery (qaṭ' al-ṭarīq). It has also been said: it is open defiance with banditry, even if it occurs in a city (miṣr). ﴿And strive upon the earth in corruption﴾ means: causing corruption. It is permissible for it (fasādan) to be in the accusative as a cause (ʿillah) or as a verbal noun (maṣdar), because their striving was corruption, so it is as if it were said: "and they corrupt upon the earth with corruption." ﴿That they be killed﴾ means: by way of retribution (qiṣāṣ), without crucifixion (ṣalb), if they committed killing alone. ﴿Or crucified﴾ means: they be crucified along with killing, if they killed and took property. Among the jurists there is disagreement over whether he is killed and crucified, or crucified alive and left, or stabbed until he dies. ﴿Or their hands and feet be cut off on opposite sides﴾: their right hands and left feet are cut off if they took property but did not kill. ﴿Or they be banished from the land﴾: they are banished from one land to another, such that they cannot settle in any place, if they were limited to intimidation. Abu Hanifa interpreted banishment (nafy) as imprisonment (ḥabs); on this reading, "or" (aw) in the verse indicates distribution (lil-tafṣīl). It has also been said that it indicates choice (lil-takhyīr), and the imam chooses among these punishments for every highway robber. ﴿That is a disgrace for them in this world﴾ meaning: humiliation and exposure. ﴿And for them in the Hereafter is a great punishment﴾ because of the greatness of their sins.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verses 34–35:

﴿Except those who repent before you have power over them﴾ is an exception specific to what is the right of Allah, glorified and exalted be He. Its evidence is His saying, exalted be He: ﴿Know that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾. As for killing in retaliation (qisas), it falls to the guardians (awliya'); its obligation (wujub) is dropped by repentance, not its permissibility (jawaz). The restriction of repentance to being prior to having power (over the offenders) indicates that repentance after having power does not drop the prescribed penalty (hadd), even though it drops the punishment (adhab). And the verse concerns highway robbers (qita' al-muslimin), because the repentance of a polytheist averts punishment from him both before and after having power.

﴿O you who believe, fear Allah and seek the means (al-wasilah) to Him﴾: that is, that by which you draw near to His reward and nearness to Him, namely performing acts of obedience and abandoning acts of disobedience. It derives from "wasala ila kadha," meaning he drew near to it. In a hadith: "al-Wasilah is a station in Paradise."

﴿And strive in His way﴾ by fighting His enemies, the outward and the inward ones. ﴿That you may succeed﴾ by arriving at Allah, glorified and exalted be He, and attaining His honour.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 36–37:

﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve, if they had whatever is on the earth⦆ of all kinds of wealth, altogether, ﴿and the like of it with it, to ransom themselves with it⦆ meaning, to make it a ransom for their own selves ﴿from the punishment of the Day of Resurrection⦆. The lam (la) is connected to an omitted element that the word law (if) requires, since the implied sense is: "if it were established that they had whatever is on the earth." The dual reference of the pronoun in bihi ("with it") to the two things mentioned is either because it is treated as the demonstrative in the manner of His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿neither old nor young, but between that⦆, or because the waw in wa-mithluhu ma'ahu ("and the like of it with it") means "with" (ma'a). ﴿It will not be accepted from them⦆ is the answer to law (if), and law together with what is in its scope is the predicate of inna (indeed), and the sentence is an illustration of the inevitability of punishment for them and that there is no way for them to escape from it. ﴿And for them is a painful punishment⦆ is an explicit statement of the intended meaning of it. Similarly is His saying: (p-126) ﴿They wish to come out of the Fire, but they will not be coming out of it, and for them is a lasting punishment⦆. It was also read as yakhrujū (from akhraja), and He said "but they will not be coming out of it" rather than "but they will not come out," for emphasis.

The Qur'an verse 38–39 commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil):

﴿As for the male thief and the female thief, cut off their hands﴾. According to Sibawayh, these are two sentences, since the implied meaning is: "In what is recited to you, the male thief and the female thief; that is, their judgment [is this]." According to al-Mubarrad, it is one sentence, and the "fa" (فاء) indicates causation. The predicate entered [the sentence] because both subjects contain the meaning of a condition, so the meaning is: "The man who stole and the woman who stole." It has also been read with the accusative (نصب), and this is the preferred reading in such constructions, because an imperative (إنشاء) cannot occur as a predicate except with an implied element and an interpretation.

Theft (السَّرِقَة) is taking another's property secretly. It requires amputation only if it is taken from a protected place (حِرْز, a secured place of storage) and the item taken is a quarter of a dinar or its equivalent in value, based on his saying (peace and blessings be upon him): "Amputation is for a quarter of a dinar or more."

The scholars differ on this, because of the hadiths that were narrated about it. I have fully examined this matter in my commentary on al-Masabih (Sharh al-Masabih). By "hands" (الأيدي) is meant the means of acquiring (الإيمان, here understood as the hands' function). This is supported by the reading of Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him): "their right hands" (أيمانهما). For this reason it is permissible to place the plural in the position of the dual, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Your hearts have indeed inclined﴾, relying on the dual of the second (genitive) noun. The word "yad" (hand) denotes the whole limb, and for this reason the Khawarij (الخوارج, an early sect) held that the place of amputation is the shoulder. The majority hold that it is the wrist (الرُّسْغ), because (peace and blessings be upon him) was brought a thief and he commanded that his right hand be cut off at the wrist.

﴿As recompense for what they earned, a punishment from Allah﴾: these two words are in the accusative, either as an object of purpose (مفعول له) or as a verbal noun (مصدر), and the verb that they depend on is implied by "cut off" (فاقطعوا). ﴿And Allah is Mighty and Wise﴾.

﴿But whoever repents﴾ from among the thieves, ﴿after his wrongdoing﴾, that is, after his theft, ﴿and makes amends﴾, meaning he strives to clear himself of the obligations (التبعات) and resolves not to return to it, ﴿then indeed Allah will turn to him in forgiveness; indeed Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾: He accepts his repentance, so He will not punish him in the Hereafter. As for the amputation, it does not lapse by repentance according to the majority, because it involves the right of the one from whom the property was stolen.
