Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 40:

﴿Do you not know that to Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth?﴾ The address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), or to everyone.

﴿He punishes whom He wills and forgives whom He wills, and Allah is over all things Competent.﴾ He placed punishment before forgiveness, following the order of what preceded it, or because the entitlement to punishment comes first, or because what is meant by it is the cutting off (of the wrongdoer), and that is in this world.

O Messenger, let not those who race to disbelief grieve you. That is, the conduct of those who fall into disbelief quickly, that is, in openly displaying it when they find an opportunity for it. ﴿Among those who say, "We believe," with their mouths, but whose hearts have not believed.﴾ That is, among the hypocrites. The preposition *bi* (with) is linked to *qalu* (they said), not to *amanna* (we believed), and the *waw* (and) may be a circumstantial clause or a conjunction. ﴿And among those who are Jews﴾ is conjoined to "among those who said." ﴿Listeners to falsehood﴾ is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "they are listeners," and the pronoun refers to both groups, or to "those who race." It is also permissible for it to be a subject, with "among those who" as its predicate, meaning: among the Jews there are people who are listeners. The *lam* in *lil-kadhib* (to falsehood) is either an emphatic extra particle, or it implies that listening carries the meaning of acceptance (*qabul*), that is, they accept what the rabbis fabricate. Or it indicates cause, with the object omitted, meaning: they listen to your speech in order to lie about it against you.

﴿Listeners to other people who have not come to you﴾: that is, listeners to another group of Jews who did not attend your gathering and kept away from you out of arrogance and extreme hatred. The meaning in both cases is: they incline toward them and accept their words, or they listen from you on their behalf and convey to them. It is also permissible for the *lam* to be linked to *al-kadhib*, because the second "listeners" is repeated for emphasis, meaning: listeners in order to lie to another people. ﴿They distort words after their places﴾: that is, they turn them away from their places where God placed them, either verbally, by altering their wording or changing their form, or in meaning, by interpreting them in other than the intended sense and applying them to other than their proper context. This sentence is another attribute of "people," or an attribute of "listeners," or a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in it, or a new independent clause with no place in the grammar, or in the nominative position as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: they distort. Likewise ﴿They say, "If you are given this, take it; but if you are not given it, beware."﴾ That is, if you are given this distorted version, accept it and act upon it. ﴿But if you are not given it﴾, rather, Muhammad has given you a ruling contrary to it, ﴿then beware﴾, that is, beware of accepting what he has ruled for you.

It has been narrated: "A nobleman from Khaybar committed adultery with a noblewoman, and both were married. They disliked stoning them, so they sent the two with a group of their people to the Banu Qurayzah, to ask the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about it. They said, 'If he orders you to flog and blacken [the faces of] them, accept it; but if he orders you to stone them, then do not.' He ordered them to be stoned, and they refused. So Ibn Suriya was made an arbiter between him and them. He said to him, 'I adjure you by God, besides whom there is no god, who split the sea for Moses, who raised the mount above you, who delivered you and drowned the family of Pharaoh, and by He who sent down to you His Book, its lawful and unlawful: do you find in it stoning for one who is married?' He said, 'Yes.' Then they leapt upon him. He said, 'I feared that if I lied to him, a punishment would descend upon us.' So the Messenger of God (ﷺ) ordered the two adulterers, and they were stoned at the gate of the mosque."

﴿And whomever God wills to be tested﴾: that is, to go astray or to be disgraced, ﴿you cannot avail him anything against God﴾: that is, you cannot prevent it for him from God. ﴿Those are the ones whose hearts God did not will to purify﴾ from disbelief. And this, as you see, is a clear text against the corrupt view of the Mu'tazilah (the rationalist school which holds that God wills only what is good for humans). ﴿For them in this world is disgrace﴾, which is that they are subjected to the poll tax (*jizya*) and fear of the believers. ﴿And for them in the Hereafter is a great punishment﴾, which is eternal abiding in the Fire. The pronoun refers to those who are Jews, if the sentence beginning "and among those who" is taken as a new clause; otherwise it refers to both groups.

﴿They are listeners to falsehood﴾: he repeated it for emphasis. ﴿They devour the unlawful gain (al-suḥt)﴾, meaning the forbidden, such as bribery. It is called suḥt, from *saḥatahu* when one uproots something, because it is *maskhūt al-barakah*, stripped of blessing. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub recited *al-suḥt* with two *ḍammas* in the three places, and these are two dialectal forms, like *al-'unuq* and *al-'unq* (both meaning "neck"). It was also recited with a *fatḥah* on the *sīn*, following the form of the verbal noun. ﴿So if they come to you, judge between them or turn away from them﴾: this is an option given to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), when they bring their disputes to him, to choose between judging and turning away. For this reason it has been said: if two People of the Book (*kitābiyyān*, Jews or Christians) bring their dispute to a judge, he is not obliged to rule between them. This is one opinion of al-Shafi'i. The more correct view, however, is that it is obligatory when the two litigants, or one of them, is a *dhimmī* (a non-Muslim living under Muslim protection), because we have undertaken to protect them and to repel injustice from them. The verse, however, does not concern the *ahl al-dhimmah*. According to Abu Hanifa, it is obligatory in all cases. ﴿And if you turn away from them, they will not harm you at all﴾: that is, by opposing you because you turn away from them, for Allah, glorified and exalted, protects you from the people. ﴿And if you judge, judge between them with justice﴾: that is, with the justice which Allah has commanded. ﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who act justly﴾: so He preserves them and magnifies their station.

"How could they make you judge while they have the Torah, in which is the judgment of Allah?" This is an expression of wonder at their appointing as judge one in whom they do not believe, while the ruling is explicitly stated in the book that they possess. It also alerts that they did not intend by the arbitration to know the truth and establish the Law, but sought only that which would be easier for them, even though, in their own claim, it was not the judgment of Allah the Exalted. "And in it is the judgment of Allah" is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) relating to the Torah if you take the word "in it" (fīhā) as a complement of location; and if you make it a subject (mubtada'), then it is governed by the pronoun hidden within it, and the feminine marking of the verb is because it is similar to the feminine in their speech in form, like mawmāh (a woman who is very beautiful) and dawdāh (a woman who is very loving). "Then they turn away after that" — then they turn away from your judgment, which agrees with their book, after the arbitration. It is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) on "they make you judge" and falls within the scope of the expression of wonder. "And those are not believers" — in their book, because of their turning away from it at first and from what agrees with it second; or in you and in it.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 44:

﴿Indeed, We sent down the Torah, in which is guidance﴾ guiding to the truth. ﴿and light﴾ that makes clear what was obscure of the rulings. ﴿by which the prophets who submitted [to Allah] judged﴾ meaning the prophets of the Children of Israel, or Musa and those after him, if we say that the law of those before us is law for us as long as it has not been abrogated (naskh), and the one who holds this position has relied on this verse. ﴿who submitted﴾ is a descriptive attribute applied to the prophets as praise for them and as an elevation of the status of the Muslims, and as an allusion to the Jews, that they are far removed from the religion of the prophets, peace be upon them, and from following their guidance. ﴿for those who were Jews﴾ is connected to "sent down," or to "judge," meaning they judge by it in their disputes, and this indicates that the prophets were their prophets. ﴿and the rabbis and the scholars﴾ their ascetics and their learned men who follow the way of their prophets, conjoined to "the prophets," ﴿by what they were entrusted with of the Book of Allah﴾ because Allah commanded them to preserve His Book from neglect and distortion; the referent of "what" is omitted, and "min" (of) is explanatory. ﴿and they were witnesses over it﴾ guardians who would not allow it to be altered, or witnesses who make clear what is hidden of it, as Ibn Suriya did. ﴿So do not fear the people, but fear Me﴾ a prohibition to the rulers from fearing other than Allah in their judgments and from compromising in them out of fear of a tyrant or regard for a powerful person. ﴿And do not exchange My verses﴾ and do not substitute for My rulings which I have sent down. ﴿for a small price﴾ which is bribery and worldly standing. And whoever does not judge by what Allah has sent down, while disdaining it and denying it. ﴿then those are the disbelievers﴾ because of their contempt for it and their rebellion by judging by other than it. For this reason He described them with the words "the disbelievers," "the wrongdoers," and "the defiantly disobedient," so their disbelief is due to their denial of it, their wrongdoing is due to judging contrary to it, and their defiant disobedience is due to departing from it. It is also possible that each of the three attributes refers to a state combined with refraining from judging by it, suitable to it, or to a group, as has been said: this one refers to the Muslims, since it is connected to their address, the "wrongdoers" refers to the Jews, and the "defiantly disobedient" refers to the Christians.

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 45:**

﴿And We prescribed for them﴾, i.e., We enjoined upon the Jews. ﴿therein﴾, i.e., in the Torah. ﴿that the life is for the life﴾, meaning that a soul is killed in return for a soul. ﴿and the eye for the eye, and the nose for the nose, and the ear for the ear, and the tooth for the tooth﴾. Al-Kisa'i read it in the nominative (*marfu'*), taking these as coordinated clauses (*jumal ma'tufah*) on *anna* and what falls within its scope, in terms of meaning, as if it were said: "We prescribed for them: the soul for the soul, and the eye for the eye," since writing and reading both apply to clauses, as they do to speech. Or they are a resumed clause (*musta'nafah*), and the meaning is: "Likewise, the eye is gouged out for the eye, the nose is slit for the nose, the ear is cut off for the ear, and the tooth is pulled out for the tooth." Or the nominative forms are coordinated with the pronoun hidden (*mustakinn*) in the phrase *bi-al-nafs*, and this was permissible because, originally, it is separated from it by the adverbial phrase, and the prepositional phrase is a clarifying circumstantial clause (*hal mubayyinah*) for the meaning. Nafi' read *wal-udhna bil-udhni* and *wa-fi udhunayhi* with the *dhal* sukun wherever it occurs. ﴿and the wounds are subject to retaliation﴾, i.e., they are subject to *qisas* (retaliation, the principle of equal retribution). Al-Kisa'i also read this in the nominative, and Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir agreed with him, on the basis that it is a summary statement of the ruling after the detailed enumeration. ﴿But whoever forgoes it﴾, i.e., from among those entitled to it. ﴿by it﴾, i.e., by the retaliation, meaning whoever pardons it. ﴿it is﴾, i.e., the forgoing. ﴿an expiation for him﴾, for the one who forgoes; God expiates his sins by it. It was also said that it is for the offender, meaning that what was incumbent upon him is removed from him. It was read: "*fa-huwa kaffaratuhu lahu*" (then it is his expiation for him), meaning: the one who forgoes, his expiation, which he deserves by the forgoing, is not diminished in any part. ﴿And whoever does not judge by what God has sent down﴾, of retaliation and other matters. ﴿those are the wrongdoers﴾.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verses 46–47:

﴿And We sent them following in their footsteps﴾, meaning: and We caused them to follow in their footsteps. The object is omitted because the prepositional phrase (*jarr wa-majrur*, the preposition with its object) indicates it. The pronoun refers to the Prophets. ﴿with ʿIsa son of Maryam﴾: this is the second object (*maf'ul thani*), to which the verb is extended by means of the preposition *bi* (with). ﴿confirming what was before him of the Torah, and We gave him the Gospel﴾: it is also recited with the *hamza* vowelled with a *fatha*. ﴿in it was guidance and light﴾: this is in the accusative position as a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*, state). ﴿and confirming what was before him of the Torah﴾ is coordinated (*'atf*) with it, and likewise His saying: ﴿and guidance and admonition for the God-fearing﴾. It is permissible to put both of these in the accusative as an object of purpose (*maf'ul lahu*), coordinated with an omitted element, or by being related to it. ﴿And let the People of the Gospel judge by what Allah has revealed in it﴾ is coordinated with "*ʿalayhi*" (upon it) in the reading of Hamza. According to the first reading, the *lam* (of purpose) is related to an omitted element, meaning: "And We gave him [the Gospel] so that he might judge." It has also been recited as "*wa-an liyahkuma*," with *an* being a conjunction governing the imperative, as in your saying, "I commanded you that stand up," meaning: "And We commanded that he judge." ﴿And whoever does not judge by what Allah has revealed, then those are the defiantly disobedient (*fasiqun*)﴾: that is, deviating from His judgment, or from faith, if one holds it in contempt. The verse indicates that the Gospel contains legal rulings, that Judaism was abrogated (*naskh*, abrogation) by the mission of ʿIsa, peace be upon him, and that he was independent in the sacred law. Whoever takes it to mean "and let them judge by what Allah has revealed in it" as requiring the practice of the rulings of the Torah is going against the apparent meaning.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verses 46–47:

﴿And We sent them following in their footsteps﴾, meaning: and We caused them to follow in their footsteps. The object is omitted because the prepositional phrase (*jarr wa-majrur*, the preposition with its object) indicates it. The pronoun refers to the Prophets. ﴿with ʿIsa son of Maryam﴾: this is the second object (*maf'ul thani*), to which the verb is extended by means of the preposition *bi* (with). ﴿confirming what was before him of the Torah, and We gave him the Gospel﴾: it is also recited with the *hamza* vowelled with a *fatha*. ﴿in it was guidance and light﴾: this is in the accusative position as a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*, state). ﴿and confirming what was before him of the Torah﴾ is coordinated (*'atf*) with it, and likewise His saying: ﴿and guidance and admonition for the God-fearing﴾. ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book in truth﴾, i.e., the Qur'an. ﴿confirming what came before it of the Book﴾, of the same kind as the revealed books. The first *al-lam* (the definite article, here marking a particular reference, *lil-'ahd*) is for a specific reference, and the second is for the genus, *lil-jins*. ﴿and as a guardian over it﴾, a watcher over all the other books, preserving it from alteration and bearing witness to its soundness and permanence. It is also read in the passive form, *muhayman 'alayhi* (هُومِنَ عَلَيْهِ), meaning that it was entrusted and was protected from distortion. The one who guards it is God, glorified and exalted, or the guardians of it in every age.

﴿So judge between them by what God has sent down﴾, i.e., by what God has sent down to you. ﴿and do not follow their desires, away from the truth that has come to you﴾, by deviating from it toward what they desire. The *'an* (عَنْ) here is connected to *lā tattabi'* because it implies the meaning of *lā tanharif* ("do not turn aside"). Alternatively, it is a circumstantial clause (*hāl*) from its subject, meaning: do not follow their desires while inclining away from what has come to you.

﴿For each of you We have appointed﴾, O people, ﴿a law (*shir'ah*)﴾, which is *sharī'ah*, and it is the path to water. The religion is likened to it because it is a path to that which is the cause of eternal life. It is also read with a *fatḥah* on the *shīn* (شَرْعَة).

﴿and a clear way (*minhāj*)﴾, and a clear path in religion, from *nahaja al-amr*, meaning when a matter became clear. From this it is inferred that we are not bound to the earlier laws (*shara'i'*).

﴿If God had willed, He would have made you one community﴾, a single group agreed upon one religion in all eras, without abrogation (*naskh*) or change. The object of *law shā'a* ("if He had willed") is omitted, and it is indicated by the answer that follows. It has also been said that the meaning is: if God had willed the gathering of you upon Islam, He would have compelled you to it. ﴿but He wants to test you in what He has given you﴾, i.e., the differing laws suited to each age and period, to see whether you will act upon them, submitting to them and believing that their differences are in accordance with divine wisdom, or whether you will turn aside from the truth and fall short in action.

﴿So race to good deeds﴾, i.e., hasten to them, seizing the opportunity and gaining the merit of precedence and advancement. ﴿To God is your return, all of you﴾, a resumed statement that gives the reason for the command to race, and a promise and a warning to those who hasten and to those who fall short. ﴿He will inform you about what you used to dispute﴾, by recompense that separates the one who is right from the one who is wrong, and the one who acts from the one who falls short.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (*Anwar al-Tanzil*) on surah 5, verse 49:

﴿And judge between them by what Allah has revealed﴾ is conjoined (*'atf*, grammatical conjunction) to "the Book," i.e., We revealed to you the Book and the judgment. Or it is conjoined to "the truth," i.e., We revealed it with the truth and [We revealed to you]: "judge between them." It is also permissible for it to be a separate clause (*jumlah*), with the implied meaning "and We commanded that you judge."

﴿And do not follow their desires, and beware of them lest they tempt you away from some of what Allah has revealed to you﴾, i.e., lest they lead you astray and turn you away from it. The clause introduced by *an* (that) is a substitute (*badal*) for "them," a substitution of inclusion (*badal al-ishtimal*), meaning "beware of their temptation." Or it is an object of purpose (*maf'ul lahu*), meaning "beware of them for fear that they will tempt you."

It was narrated: "The rabbis of the Jews said: 'Come, let us go to Muhammad, perhaps we can tempt him away from his religion.' So they said: 'O Muhammad, you know that we are the rabbis of the Jews, and that if we follow you, all the Jews will follow us. Indeed, there is a dispute between us and our people, so we will bring it to your judgment, and you will decide in our favor against them, and we will believe in you and affirm you.' But the Messenger of Allah ﷺ refused that, and so this was revealed."

﴿But if they turn away﴾ from the revealed judgment and desire something other than it. ﴿Know that Allah only intends to afflict them for some of their sins﴾, meaning the sin of turning away from the judgment of Allah, glorified and exalted is He. He expressed it this way to alert (*tanbih*) that they have many sins, and this one, despite its gravity, is only one of them, counted among the whole. This also indicates magnification (*ta'zim*), as in the indefinite form (*tankir*). A parallel to this is the verse of Labid:

*Or some souls are bound by their rest (jimamuha)*

﴿And indeed, many of the people are defiantly disobedient﴾, rebellious in disbelief and transgressing therein.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 50:

﴿Do they then seek the judgement of the Jahiliyyah (the age of ignorance)?﴾ This refers to inclination and flattery in judgement. What is meant by "al-Jahiliyyah" is the Jahili creed (al-millah al-jahiliyyah), which is following one's desires. It is said that it was revealed concerning the Banu Qurayzah and al-Nadir, who asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to judge by what the people of the Jahiliyyah used to judge by, namely favouring one group over another in the matter of the slain. It is also read as "ḥukma" (with the ḥukm in the nominative) as a subject (mubtada'), with "yabghūna" as its predicate (khabar), and the returning pronoun (al-rāji') is omitted, which he omitted in the relative clause in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Is this the one whom Allah has sent as a messenger?﴾ This is considered weak outside of poetry. It is also read "afa-ḥukmi al-Jahiliyyati", meaning: they seek a ruler like the rulers of the Jahiliyyah, who judges according to their whims. Ibn 'Amir read "tabghūna" with the ta', as if it were said: "Say to them: Do you seek the judgement of the Jahiliyyah?" ﴿And who is better in judgement than Allah for a people who are certain?﴾ That is, in their estimation. The lam is for clarification, as in His words, exalted is He: ﴿Hayta laka﴾ (come, I am at your disposal). That is, this question is for a people who are certain, for they are the ones who reflect upon matters and verify things by their insight, so they know that there is no better judgement than Allah's, glorified and exalted is He.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 51:

﴿O you who believe, do not take the Jews and the Christians as allies﴾ So do not rely on them, and do not associate with them in the manner of intimate friends. ﴿They are allies of one another﴾ This is an indication of the reason (ʿillah) for the prohibition, meaning: they are united against you, one of them allies with another because of their unity in religion and their consensus in opposing you. ﴿And whoever among you allies with them, then he is one of them﴾ That is, whoever among you takes them as allies is one of their number. This emphasis is due to the obligation to keep away from them, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Their fires should not see each other." Or, it is because those who allied with them were hypocrites. ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people﴾ That is, those who wronged themselves by allying with the disbelievers, or the believers who wronged them by allying with their enemies.(p-131)

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 52:**

﴿So you see those in whose hearts is a disease⦆ means Ibn Ubayy and his like. ﴿They hasten toward them⦆ means, in their allegiance to them and their support of them.

﴿They say, "We fear that a reversal of fortune may befall us."⦆ They make an excuse, claiming that they fear a misfortune of the vicissitudes of time, that the matter will turn around and the state will belong to the disbelievers.

It is narrated that ʿUbadah ibn al-Samit (may Allah be pleased with him) said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "I have many clients among the Jews, in number, and I disavow their allegiance before Allah and His Messenger, and I take Allah and His Messenger as my allies." Then Ibn Ubayy said: "I am a man who fears reversals, and I will not disavow the allegiance of my clients." So this was revealed.

﴿Perhaps Allah will bring a victory⦆ for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) over his enemies and the manifestation of the Muslims. ﴿Or a decision from Him⦆ that uproots the root of the Jews through killing and expulsion, or the command to expose the secrets of the hypocrites and kill them. ﴿Then they will become⦆ meaning these hypocrites. ﴿regretful for what they concealed within themselves⦆ regarding what they harbored of disbelief and doubt concerning the matter of the Messenger (ﷺ), in addition to what they displayed that indicated their hypocrisy.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 53:

﴿And those who believe say⁠﴾ — with the nominative (al-raf') reading of ʿĀṣim, Ḥamzah and al-Kisāʾī, on the basis that it is an independent statement (kalām mubtadaʾ). It is corroborated by the reading of Ibn Kathīr, Nāfiʿ and Ibn ʿĀmir, which is nominative without a waw, on the basis that it is the answer to a questioner who says: "Then what do the believers say at that time?" The accusative reading is that of Abū ʿAmr and Yaʿqūb, coordinated (ʿaṭfan) with an-yaʾtiya (that He bring) with regard to meaning; it is as if he said: "It is hoped that Allah brings victory and that those who believe say..." Or he makes it a substitute (badal) for the name of Allah, Exalted is He, included in the subject of ʿasā, the predicate being dispensed with by what it contains of the event (ḥadath). Or it is in the accusative on the basis of the meaning: "It is hoped that Allah brings victory and the saying of the believers, for bringing about what necessitates it is like bringing about the thing itself."

﴿Are these the ones who swore by Allah with the utmost of their oaths, that they are truly with you?⁠﴾ The believers say this to one another, marvelling at the state of the hypocrites and boasting of the sincerity (al-ikhlāṣ) with which Allah, Glorified and Exalted, has favoured them. Or they say it to the Jews, since the hypocrites had sworn to them of support, as Allah, Exalted is He, related of them. ﴿And if you are fought, we will surely help you⁠﴾. The utmost of oaths (jahd al-aymān) is the most emphatic of them. It is in origin a verbal noun (maṣdar), and it is put in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl), on the estimate: "and they swore by Allah, striving with the striving of their oaths," so the verb was deleted and the verbal noun was placed in its stead. For this reason it was permissible for it to be definite. Or it is in the accusative as an absolute object (maṣdar), since it carries the meaning of "they swore."

﴿Their deeds have become void, and they have become losers⁠﴾. It is either part of what is said, or it is a statement of Allah, Glorified and Exalted, as a testimony to them of the voiding of their deeds; and in it there is the sense of wonder, as if it were said: "He has voided their deeds, how much of a loss they are!"

O you who believe, whoever among you turns back from his religion (﴿مَن يَرْتَدَّ مِنكم عَنْ دِينِهِ﴾)... Nafi' and Ibn Amir read it in its original form (ʿalā al-aṣl, without idgham, i.e., without assimilating the two consonants), and it is so in the ʿUthmanic codex (al-Imam). The rest read it with idgham (assimilation, merging the two identical consonants into one). This is among the unseen matters that Allah the Exalted informed of before they occurred. Three groups of the Arabs apostatized toward the end of the lifetime of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ):

The Banu Mudlij, whose chief was Dhu'l-Himar al-Aswad al-Ansi (ذو الحمار الأسود العنسي). He claimed prophethood in Yemen and seized its lands. Then Fayruz al-Daylami killed him the night after the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) passed away. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was informed of this during that same night, so the Muslims rejoiced, and the news arrived at the end of Rabi' al-Awwal.

The Banu Hanifa, the followers of Musaylima, who claimed prophethood. He wrote to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "From Musaylima, the messenger of Allah, to Muhammad, the messenger of Allah (ﷺ). To proceed: the earth is half mine and half yours." The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) replied to Musaylima the Liar: "To proceed: the earth belongs to Allah; He bestows it upon whomever He wills of His servants, and the good end is for the righteous." Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) fought him with a force of Muslims, and Wahshi, the slayer of Hamza, killed him.

The Banu Asad, the people of Tulayha ibn Khuwaylid, who claimed prophethood. (p-132) The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent Khalid against him. He fled to Syria after the fighting, then embraced Islam and his Islam became good.

In the time of Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him), seven groups apostatized: Fazara, the people of Uyayna ibn Hisn; Ghatafan, the people of Firra ibn Salama al-Qushayri; the Banu Sulaym, the people of al-Fujaa'a ibn Abd Yalil; the Banu Yarbu', the people of Malik ibn Nuwayra; part of Tamim, the people of Sajah bint al-Mundhir, the prophetess who was the wife of Musaylima; Kinda, the people of al-Ash'ath ibn Qays; and the Banu Bakr ibn Wa'il in Bahrayn, the people of al-Hatm ibn Zayd. Allah sufficed them through his hand. In the leadership of Umar ibn al-Khattab (may Allah be pleased with him), Ghassan, the people of Jabala ibn al-Ayham, became Christian and went to Syria.

﴿فَسَوْفَ يَأْتِي اللَّهُ بِقَوْمٍ يُحِبُّهم ويُحِبُّونَهُ﴾ (So Allah will bring a people whom He loves and who love Him). It was said they are the people of Yemen, based on what is narrated: "that he (upon him be prayers and peace) gestured toward Abu Musa al-Ash'ari and said: They are the people of this man."

It was also said they are the Persians, because he (upon him be prayers and peace) "was asked about them, so he struck his hand on the shoulder of Salman and said: This one and his people."

It was also said they are those who fought at the Battle of al-Qadisiyya: two thousand from al-Nakha', five thousand from Kinda and Bujayla, and three thousand from the mixed tribes of people. The pronoun referring back to "from" (man) is elided; its estimated form is: "then Allah will bring a people in their place." Allah's love for His servants means His will for their guidance and success in this world and good reward in the Hereafter; and the servants' love for Him means their will to obey Him and to guard against His disobedience.

﴿أذِلَّةٍ عَلى المُؤْمِنِينَ﴾ (humble toward the believers): being compassionate toward them and humbling themselves before them. It is the plural of dhalil (ذليل), not dhalul (ذلول), since its plural is dhulul. Its use with ʿalā (عَلى) is either because it includes the meaning of tenderness and affection, or to alert that they, despite their high rank and superiority over the believers, are submissive to them, or for contrast.

﴿أعِزَّةٍ عَلى الكافِرِينَ﴾ (mighty against the disbelievers): stern, prevailing over them, from ʿazzahu (عزّه), meaning he overcame him. It was also read in the accusative (aʿizzatan) as a circumstantial state (ḥāl).

﴿يُجاهِدُونَ في سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ﴾ (they strive in the way of Allah) is another attribute of the people, or a circumstantial state of the pronoun in aʿizzah. ﴿وَلا يَخافُونَ لَوْمَةَ لائِمٍ﴾ (and they fear not the blame of any blamer) is conjoined to yujāhidūn, meaning they combine striving in the way of Allah with firmness in His religion; or it is a state, meaning they are strivers whose condition is contrary to that of the hypocrites, who go out with the army of the Muslims fearing the blame of their allies among the Jews, so they do nothing that would incur blame from them. The lawmah (لومة) is a single instance of blame, and there are two forms of emphasis in it and in the indefiniteness of lā'im (لائم).

﴿ذَلِكَ﴾ (that) refers to the attributes mentioned before. ﴿فَضْلُ اللَّهِ يُؤْتِيهِ مَن يَشاءُ﴾ (It is the bounty of Allah; He gives it to whom He wills): He grants it and enables him to attain it. ﴿واللَّهُ واسِعٌ﴾ (And Allah is All-Encompassing): abundant in bounty. ﴿عَلِيمٌ﴾ (All-Knowing) of whoever is worthy of it.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verses 55–56:

﴿Your only walī (guardian, protector, ally) is Allah, and His Messenger, and those who believe﴾. When He had forbidden taking the disbelievers as allies (walāya), He mentioned right after it the one who truly deserves that role. He said "your walī is Allah" rather than "your awliyā'" (guardians, plural) to draw attention to the fact that guardianship belongs to Allah, Glorified and Exalted, in the primary sense, and to His Messenger (ﷺ) and the believers in a secondary sense, by way of following.

﴿Who establish the prayer and give the zakāt (obligatory alms)﴾ is a qualifying description (ṣifa) of "those who believe," since it functions as a noun (ism), or it is a substitute (badal) for it. It is also permissible to put it in the accusative or nominative for the sake of praise.

﴿And they are bowing (rāki'ūn)﴾: humbly submissive in their prayer and their zakāt. It has also been said that it is a specific circumstantial clause (ḥāl makhṣūṣa) relating to "they give," meaning: they give zakāt while bowing in prayer, out of eagerness for doing good and hastening to it. It is said that this verse was revealed concerning ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him), when a beggar asked him while he was bowing in his prayer, and he gave him his ring.

The Shia (al-Shīʿa, the partisans of ʿAlī) used this verse as evidence for his imamate (imāma, leadership), claiming that "walī" means the one who manages affairs and has the right to dispose of them. The apparent meaning is what we have mentioned. Moreover, reading a plural form as referring to one person is also contrary to the apparent meaning. Even if it is authentically reported that it was revealed about him, the plural form may have been used to encourage people to act as he did, so that they would be included in it. On this basis, the verse is evidence that a small action during prayer does not invalidate it, and that voluntary charity is also called zakāt.

﴿And whoever takes Allah, His Messenger, and those who believe as allies﴾: and whoever takes them as awliyā' (protectors).

﴿Then indeed the party of Allah, they are the victorious﴾: that is, indeed they are the victorious. However, placing the apparent noun in the position of the pronoun serves to draw attention to the proof for it. It is as if it were said: whoever takes these as allies, they are the party of Allah, and the party of Allah are the victorious. It also serves to honour them by mentioning them, to glorify their status, to ennoble them with this title, and to hint at those who take as allies others than these, that they are the party of Satan. The root of ḥizb is a people who gather for a matter that unites them.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 57:

﴿O you who have believed, do not take those who have taken your religion as ridicule and amusement from among those who were given the Scripture before you, nor the disbelievers, as allies﴾ It was revealed concerning Rifa'a ibn Zayd and Suwayd ibn al-Harith, who displayed Islam and then became hypocrites, and some men among the Muslims used to befriend them. He tied the prohibition of allying with them to their taking their religion as ridicule and amusement, as an indication of the cause and an alert that whoever has such a condition is far from allegiance and deserves enmity and hatred. The separation of "those who ridicule" from "the People of the Book and the disbelievers" is according to the reading of the one who put it in the genitive (jarra), namely Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub. The word "disbelievers" (kuffar), although it includes the People of the Book, is applied specifically to the polytheists because their disbelief is doubled. And the one who put it in the accusative (nasaba) made it a conjunct of "those who have taken," on the basis that the prohibition concerns allying with anyone who is not upon the truth at all, whether he is a person of a religion who follows his desire and distorts it from the right, like the People of the Book, or one who is not, like the polytheists. ﴿And fear God﴾ by abandoning the prohibited acts. ﴿If you are believers﴾ because true faith necessitates that. It has also been said: "If you are believers in His promise and His threat."

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 58:

﴿And when you call to the prayer, they take it as a mockery and a game.﴾ That is, they took the prayer (as a mockery and a game), or the calling (to it). In this is evidence that the adhan (call to prayer) is prescribed for the prayer.

It is narrated that a Christian in Medina, whenever he heard the muezzin say, "I bear witness that Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ)," would say, "May Allah burn the liar." Then one night his servant came in with a fire while his family was asleep, and its sparks scattered in the house and burned him and his family.

﴿That is because they are a people who do not reason.﴾ For foolishness leads to ignorance of the truth and to mocking it, whereas reason prevents one from it.

**﴿Say, "O People of the Scripture, do you find fault with us?"﴾** Do you disapprove of us and criticize us? It is said *naqima minhu kadha* (نَقِمَ مِنهُ كَذا) when one disapproves of something, and *intaqama* (انْتَقَمَ) when one repays someone. It was also read *tanqamuna* (تَنْقَمُونَ) with a fatha on the *qaf*, and this is a dialectal variant.

**﴿Only because we believe in God and in what has been revealed to us and what was revealed before,﴾** meaning belief in all the revealed books. **﴿and that most of you are defiantly disobedient.﴾** This is conjoined (*ʿuṭifa*, عُطِفَ) to *an āmannā* (أنْ آمَنّا). The exception appears to govern both matters together, which is non-compliance. The meaning is: you find fault with us only for our non-compliance, since we have entered into faith while you remain outside it. Alternatively, the original phrase was "and the belief that most of you are defiantly disobedient," and the governing noun has been omitted. Or the construction is *ʿalā mā*, meaning: "You find fault with us only for believing in God and in what He revealed, and for [the fact] that most of you are defiantly disobedient." Or there is an omitted cause, and the sense is: "Do you find fault with us only because we believed, owing to your lack of fairness and your defiance?" Or it is in the accusative, governed by an implied verb indicated by *hal tanqimūna* (هَلْ تَنْقِمُونَ): "and you do not find fault with the fact that most of you are defiantly disobedient." Or it is in the nominative, as a new sentence with an omitted predicate: "and your defiance is established and known to you, but love of leadership and wealth prevents you from being fair."

The verse addresses the Jews, who asked the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about whom he believed in. He said: "I believe in God and in what has been revealed to us," up to His words, "and to Him we are submitting." When they heard the mention of Jesus, they said: "We know of no religion worse than your religion."

Say: "Shall I inform you of something worse than that retribution (al-manqum)?" That is, worse than that which was requited.

**"Mathūbah"** (reward, recompense) **in the sight of Allah**: a recompense established with Allah, glorified and exalted be He. The word *mathūbah* is specific to good, just as *'uqūbah* (punishment) is specific to evil, so it is placed here in the position of *'uqūbah*, following the manner of the poet's saying:

"Their greeting among them is a striking blow, and a painful one." (p-134)

He has put it in the accusative as a *tamyīz* (specification) following *bi-sharrin* ("something worse").

**"Whom Allah has cursed and with whom He became angry, and from whom He made apes and swine"**: this is a *badal* (substitute) for *bi-sharrin*, with an omitted modifier, meaning: "worse than the people of that is the one whom Allah has cursed." Or: "worse than that is the religion of the one whom Allah has cursed." Or it is a omitted predicate, meaning: "it is the one whom Allah has cursed, and they are the Jews, whom Allah has removed far from His mercy and against whom He became wrathful because of their disbelief and their persistence in sins after the signs had become clear. He transformed some of them into apes, and they were the people of the Sabbath, and some of them into swine, and they were the disbelievers among the people of the table of 'Īsā, upon him be peace." It has also been said that both transformations concerned the people of the Sabbath: their young men were made into apes and their elders into swine.

**"And worshipped the Ṭāghūt"**: this is coordinated (*'uṭifa*) with the relative clause (*ṣilah*) of *man* ("whoever"). Likewise, *'ubida al-ṭāghūt* is read with the passive voice and the *ṭāghūt* in the nominative, with *'ubida* meaning "became worshipped," so that the returning pronoun is omitted, meaning "among them" or "between them." Whoever reads *"wa-'ābid al-ṭāghūt"* or *"wa-'abid"* takes it as an adjective like *faṭin* and *yaqiẓ*, or as *'abadah* (plural), or *'abad al-ṭāghūt* as a plural like *khadam*, or the original form is *'abadah*, with the *tā'* dropped for the *iḍāfah* (annexation). He has coordinated it with *al-qiradah* ("the apes"). Whoever reads *"wa-'abadi al-ṭāghūt"* in the genitive coordinates it with *man*. By *al-ṭāghūt* is meant the calf; it has also been said that it means the soothsayers, and everyone who obeyed them in disobedience to Allah, exalted be He.

**"Those"** (*ulā'ika*), that is, the cursed ones. **"Are worse in position"**: He made their position worse so that it would be more emphatic in indicating their evil. It has also been said that *makānan* is indeclinable (*munṣarif*) in this reading. **"And further astray from the right way"**: from the intended, moderate path, between the excess of the Christians and the defamation of the Jews. The intent of the two comparative forms is an increase in absolute terms, not relative to the believers in evil and misguidance.

Revealed concerning the Jews who were hypocritical toward the Messenger of God (ﷺ), or concerning the hypocrites in general. ﴿When they come to you, they say, "We believe."﴾ ﴿And they entered with disbelief, and they went out with it.﴾ That is, they leave your presence as they entered it: what they heard from you has had no effect on them. The two clauses are circumstantial clauses (ḥāl, a clause describing the state of the subject) relating to the subject of *qālū* ("they said"). *Bil-kufr* ("with disbelief") and *bihi* ("with it") are circumstantial phrases relating to the subjects of *dakhalū* ("they entered") and *kharajū* ("they went out"). The particle *qad* when it precedes a past verb brings the past close to the present so that the clause can function as a ḥāl. Because of the expectation it carries, *qad* also indicates that the signs of hypocrisy were already apparent upon them, and the Messenger (ﷺ) was suspecting this. Therefore he said: ﴿And God knows best what they were concealing,﴾ meaning of disbelief. In this is a warning (waʿīd) to them.

﴿And you see many of them﴾ meaning of the Jews, or of the hypocrites. ﴿Hastening into sin﴾ meaning into what is forbidden. It has been said that it means falsehood, based on His saying: ﴿"...from their speaking of sin"﴾. ﴿And transgression﴾ meaning injustice, or exceeding the limit in acts of disobedience. It has also been said that *al-ithm* (sin) is what pertains specifically to them, and *al-ʿudwān* (transgression) is what extends to others. ﴿And their consuming of what is unlawful (al-suḥt)﴾ meaning what is forbidden; he singled it out for mention for emphasis. ﴿Evil indeed is what they were doing.﴾ That is, evil indeed is the thing they did.

Verse 63: ﴿Why do the rabbis and the scholars not forbid them from their uttering of sin and their consuming of what is unlawful?﴾ This is a reproach (tahdid) to their scholars to forbid them from that. For "lawla" (why not) when it precedes a past verb conveys reproach (tawbikh), and when it precedes a future verb conveys urging (tahdid). ﴿Evil indeed is what they used to do.﴾ This is more emphatic than His saying "evil indeed is what they used to work (ya'malun)", in that "sun'" (craftsmanship, doing) is a person's action after training in it, deliberation, and careful pursuit of excellence (ijada). For this reason He censured their elite with it. Also, neglecting enjoining the good and forbidding the evil (hisba) is worse than committing the sin, because the self takes pleasure in it and inclines toward it, whereas abstaining from condemning it is not like that; so it deserves the most severe censure.

(p-135) ﴿And the Jews said: "The hand of Allah is chained up."﴾ That is, He is withholding, restricting provision. Tightening the hand (ghull al-yad) and opening it (basṭuhā) is a metaphor (majāz) for stinginess and generosity, and there is no intention to affirm an actual hand, chain, or outstretching. For this reason it is used where such a thing cannot be imagined, as in the verse:

Generous was the pasture-land, its hands outstretched with abundant rain,
its high plains and low valleys gave thanks for its bounty.

Its counterpart among compound metaphors is: "the dark locks of the night have grayed." It has also been said that its meaning is that He is poor, based on His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Allah has indeed heard the saying of those who said: "Allah is poor and we are rich."﴾ ﴿Their hands are chained up, and they are cursed for what they said.﴾ This is a supplication against them with stinginess and misery, or with poverty and need; or it may be that their hands are literally chained, as they are shackled as captives in this world and dragged to the Fire in the Hereafter. In that case the correspondence (muṭābaqa) is in the wording and in consideration of the origin, like your saying: "He cursed me, may Allah cut off his remnant."

﴿Rather, both His hands are outstretched.﴾ He mentioned the hand in dual form for emphasis in the rebuttal, and to negate stinginess from Him, Exalted is He, and to affirm the utmost generosity, since the furthest a generous person can give from his wealth is to give it with his own two hands. It is also an indication of the giving of this world and the Hereafter, and of what He gives as a lure (istidrāj) and what He gives as an honor (ikrām).

﴿He spends as He wills.﴾ This is an emphasis on that: that is, He is free in His giving, expanding at one time and restricting at another according to His will and the requirement of His wisdom, not in a sequence of abundance and constriction arising from a state of means. It is not permissible to make it a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun (hā') in "yadāhu," because of the separation between them by the predicate, and because the pronoun is a mudāf ilayhi; nor from "yadayn" (the two hands), since there is no pronoun in them for it to refer to; nor from their pronoun for that reason.

The verse was revealed concerning Finḥāṣ ibn ʿĀzūrāʾ, for he said this when Allah withheld from the Jews the abundance He had extended to them, because of the evil consequence of their denial of Muḥammad (ﷺ). Others shared in this saying, because they were content with his words. ﴿And surely many of them will increase in transgression and disbelief through what has been revealed to you from your Lord.﴾ That is, they are transgressors and disbelievers, and they increase in transgression and disbelief through what they hear of the Qur'an, just as a sick person increases in sickness from eating food suitable only for the healthy.

﴿And We have placed among them enmity and hatred until the Day of Resurrection.﴾ So their hearts do not agree and their statements do not coincide.

﴿Whenever they kindle a fire for war, Allah extinguishes it.﴾ Whenever they intended war against the Messenger (ﷺ) and stirred up evil against him, Allah, Glorified and Exalted is He, repelled them by causing strife among them, by which He restrained their evil from him. Or: whenever they intended war against anyone, they were defeated, for when they opposed the judgment of the Torah, Allah set Bukhtnaṣr (Nebuchadnezzar) over them; then they corrupted again, so He set Faṭrus the Roman over them; then they corrupted again, so He set the Magians over them; then they corrupted again, so He set the Muslims over them. The phrase "lil-ḥarb" (for war) is connected either to "awqadū" or is an attribute of "nāran" (a fire).

﴿And they strive in the land to cause corruption﴾, that is, for corruption, which is their diligence in scheming, stirring up wars and strife, and violating what is sacred.

﴿And Allah does not love the corrupters﴾, so He will not repay them except with evil.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verses 65–66:

﴿And if the People of the Book had believed﴾ in Muhammad (ﷺ) and in what he brought, ﴿and had feared God﴾ [i.e., avoided] the sins we have enumerated and the like.

﴿We would have expiated from them their misdeeds﴾ that they committed, and We would not have punished them for them. ﴿And We would have admitted them into Gardens of Bliss﴾, and We would have made them among those who enter them.

In this there is an alert to the greatness of their sins and the abundance of their wrongdoings, and that Islam effaces what came before it, however great it may be, and that the People of the Book do not enter Paradise unless they embrace Islam.

﴿And if they had upheld the Torah and the Gospel﴾ by broadcasting what is in them of the description of Muhammad, peace be upon him, and by standing by their rulings, ﴿and what was sent down to them from their Lord﴾ — meaning the rest of the revealed books, since they are obligated to believe in them just as in what was sent down to them — or the Qur'an, ﴿they would have eaten from above them and from beneath their feet﴾: He would have expanded their provisions by pouring upon them blessings from the heaven and the earth, or by increasing the fruit of the trees and the yield of the crops, or by granting them gardens with luscious fruits, so that they would pick them from the top of the tree and gather what has fallen onto the ground. Thereby He made clear that what was withheld from them was due to the evil of their disbelief and their sins, not to any deficiency in the outpouring; and if they had believed and upheld what they were commanded, He would have expanded for them and granted them the good of both abodes. ﴿Among them is a moderate community﴾ (p-136): just, not extreme nor negligent, and they are those who believed in Muhammad (ﷺ). It has also been said that "moderate" means moderate in their enmity towards him. ﴿But many of them—evil is what they do﴾: that is, wretched is what they do; and in it is the sense of wonder, i.e., how bad is their deed, which is obstinacy, distorting the truth, turning away from it, and excess in enmity.

﴿And if the People of the Book had believed﴾ in Muhammad (ﷺ) and in what he brought, ﴿and had feared God﴾ [i.e., avoided] the sins we have enumerated and the like.

﴿We would have expiated from them their misdeeds﴾ that they committed, and We would not have punished them for them. ﴿And We would have admitted them into Gardens of Bliss﴾, and We would have made them among those who enter them.

In this there is an alert to the greatness of their sins and the abundance of their wrongdoings, and that Islam effaces what came before it, however great it may be, and that the People of the Book do not enter Paradise unless they embrace Islam.

﴿And if they had upheld the Torah and the Gospel﴾ by broadcasting what is in them of the description of Muhammad, peace be upon him, and by standing by their rulings, ﴿and what was sent down to them from their Lord﴾ — meaning the rest of the revealed books, since they are obligated to believe in them just as in what was sent down to them — or the Qur'an, ﴿they would have eaten from above them and from beneath their feet﴾: He would have expanded their provisions by pouring upon them blessings from the heaven and the earth, or by increasing the fruit of the trees and the yield of the crops, or by granting them gardens with luscious fruits, so that they would pick them from the top of the tree and gather what has fallen onto the ground. Thereby He made clear that what was withheld from them was due to the evil of their disbelief and their sins, not to any deficiency in the outpouring; and if they had believed and upheld what they were commanded, He would have expanded for them and granted them the good of both abodes. ﴿Among them is a moderate community﴾ (p-136): just, not extreme nor negligent, and they are those who believed in Muhammad (ﷺ). It has also been said that "moderate" means moderate in their enmity towards him. ﴿But many of them—evil is what they do﴾: that is, wretched is what they do; and in it is the sense of wonder, i.e., how bad is their deed, which is obstinacy, distorting the truth, turning away from it, and excess in enmity.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 67:

﴿O Messenger, proclaim that which has been revealed to you from your Lord﴾ all of what has been revealed to you, without being concerned about anyone or fearing any harm.

﴿But if you do not﴾ if you do not convey all of it as I have commanded you. ﴿then you have not conveyed His message﴾ then you have not delivered any part of it, because concealing some of it nullifies what has been delivered of it, just as abandoning some of the pillars (arkan) of prayer (salah) invalidates it, for the purpose of the call (da'wah) is undermined by it. Or it means: it is as if you had not conveyed any part of it, like His saying: ﴿it is as if he had slain mankind entirely﴾, since concealing part and concealing all are equal in terms of forfeiting intercession and inviting punishment.

Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Abu Bakr read ﴿risalatihi﴾ (His messages) in the plural with a kasra on the ta'. ﴿And Allah will protect you from the people﴾ a promise and guarantee from Allah, glorified and exalted be He, of protecting the person of His Messenger ﷺ from the attacks of enemies, and a removal of their excuses. ﴿Indeed, Allah does not guide the disbelieving people﴾ He will not enable them to do what they wish against you.

And from the Prophet ﷺ: "Allah sent me with His messages, and I felt constrained by them, so Allah the Exalted revealed to me: 'If you do not convey My message, I will punish you.' He guaranteed me protection, and so I grew strong."

And from Anas, may Allah be pleased with him: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to be guarded until this was revealed. Then he put his head out of a leather tent and said: 'Disperse, O people, for Allah has protected me from the people.'"

The apparent meaning of the verse requires the conveying of everything that has been revealed, though perhaps what is meant is the conveying of what concerns the welfare of the servants, and the purpose of its revelation is to make them aware of it, since among the divine secrets is that which it is forbidden to disclose.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 68:

﴿Say: O People of the Scripture, you are not upon anything﴾, meaning, no religion that is considered valid or that may rightly be called "anything," because it is false. ﴿Until you establish the Torah and the Gospel and what has been revealed to you from your Lord﴾. Among establishing them is faith in Muhammad (ﷺ) and submission to his judgment, for all the divine books together command belief in whoever confirms them, and the miracle speaks clearly of the obligation to obey him. What is intended is the establishment of their foundations (usul) and of those of their rulings (furu') that have not been abrogated (naskh). ﴿But what has been revealed to you from your Lord will surely increase many of them in transgression and disbelief. So do not grieve over the disbelieving people﴾, meaning, do not grieve over them because of the increase in their transgression and disbelief at what you convey to them, for the harm of that reaches them and does not pass them by, and among the believers there is an alternative for you apart from them.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 69:

﴿Indeed, those who believe, and those who are Jews, and the Sabians, and the Christians﴾ Its explanation has already passed in Surah al-Baqarah. "Al-Sabi'un" is in the nominative case by way of inception (al-ibtida'), and its predicate is omitted, and the intention in it is postponement of what is within the scope of "inna" (the particle of emphasis). The implied sense is: "Indeed, those who believe, and those who are Jews, and the Christians, their ruling is such-and-such, and the Sabians likewise," like his saying:

"So indeed I and Qayyar therein are strangers"

and his saying:

"And otherwise, know that we and you are rebellious transgressors, so long as we remain in dissension"

That is, "Know that we are transgressors and you are likewise," and it is like a parenthetical remark, by which he indicates that since the Sabians, despite the clear manifestness of their misguidance and their deviation from all religions, are still granted repentance if faith and righteous deeds are sound from them, others are more deserving of this. It is permissible that "wa al-Nasara" (and the Christians) be conjoined to it (the subject of inna), and "man amana" (whoever believes) be the predicate of both, and the predicate of "inna" is implied, indicated by what follows it, like his saying:

"We are with what we have, and you are with what you have, content, though the opinion differs"

It is not permissible to conjoin it to the place (mahall) of "inna" and its noun, for that is conditioned upon completing the predicate; for if it were conjoined to it before the predicate, the predicate would be the predicate of both the subject and of "inna" together, and two governing elements would converge on it. Nor is it permissible to conjoin it to the pronoun in "hadu" (they became Jews), due to the absence of emphasis and separation, and because that would necessitate that the Sabians be Jews. It has been said that "inna" here means "na'am" (yes), and what follows it is in the place of nominative by inception. It has also been said that "al-Sabi'una" is in the accusative with a fatha, and just as it was permitted to be marked with the ya', it is permitted to be marked with the waw. ﴿Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day and does righteous deeds﴾ is in the place of nominative by inception, with its predicate. ﴿There shall be no fear for them, nor shall they grieve﴾ and the sentence is the predicate of "inna" or the predicate of the subject, as has passed, and the returning pronoun is omitted, meaning: whoever of them believes. Or it is in the accusative as a substitute (badal) for the noun of "inna" and what is conjoined to it. It is recited "al-Sabi'in" (in the genitive), which is the apparent reading, and "al-Sabiyyun" with the hamza changed to ya', and "al-Sabun" with its deletion, from "saba" by replacing the hamza with alif, or from "sabawtu," because they inclined toward pursuing desires and did not follow any law or reason.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 70:

﴿Indeed We took the covenant of the Children of Israel and sent to them messengers.﴾ So that they would remind them and would make clear to them the matter of their religion. ﴿Every time a messenger came to them with what their souls did not desire,﴾ that is, with what contradicts their whims of the sacred laws and the hardships of the obligations. ﴿A group they denied and a group they killed.﴾ The answer to the conditional (kullama, "every time") is this, and the clause is a qualifier (sifah) of "messengers," with a returning pronoun omitted, i.e., "a messenger from among them." It has also been said that the answer is omitted, indicated by this clause, and that this is a resumptive statement (isti'naf). The verb "yaqtulun" (they kill) was used in place of "qatalu" (they killed) to depict the past situation (hikayat al-hal al-madiyah), to bring it vividly to mind (istihdaran laha), to express the horror of the killing (istifdha'an lil-qatl), to alert that this was their habit both in the past and in the future (tanbihan 'ala anna dhalika min daydanihim madiyan wa mustaqbalan), and to preserve the rhyme of the verse endings (muhafadhatan 'ala ru'us al-ayi).

Commentary of al-Baydawi (*Anwar al-Tanzil*) on surah 5, verse 71:

﴿And they thought there would be no trial﴾, meaning: the Children of Israel thought that they would not be afflicted with calamity and punishment for killing the prophets and denying them.

Abu 'Amr, Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Ya'qub read *lā takūnu* with a *ḍamma* (*rafʿ*), on the basis that the *an* is the lightened form of the heavy *anna* (*an al-mukhaffafa min al-thaqīla*). Its original form was *annahu lā takūnu fitnatun*, so *anna* was lightened and the pronoun of the matter (*ḍamīr al-shaʾn*) was omitted, becoming *an lā takūna*. The verb of thinking (*ḥusbān*) was placed upon it, and this particle is for affirmation (*lil-taḥqīq*), treating the thinking as if it were knowledge, so that it would be firmly fixed in their hearts. *Anna* or *an*, together with what follows it in its clause, takes the place of both of the verb's objects.

﴿So they were blind﴾ to the religion, or to the proofs and guidance. ﴿and deaf﴾ to listening to the truth, as they did when they worshipped the calf.

﴿Then Allah turned to them﴾, meaning: then they repented, and Allah turned to them in forgiveness. ﴿Then many of them became blind and deaf again﴾, a second time.

It was also read with *ḍamma* on both verbs (*ʿammāhum wa-ṣammahum*), on the basis that Allah made them blind and deaf, that is, struck them with blindness and deafness. This reading is rare; the common usage is *aʿmā* and *aṣamm*.

﴿Many of them﴾ is either a substitute (*badal*) for the pronoun, or the subject (*fāʿil*) with the *wāw* as a plural marker, as in the saying of people: *akalūnī al-barāghīth* ("the fleas ate me"); or it is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: "the blindness and the deafness are many among them."

It has also been said that it is a subject (*mubtadaʾ*) and the clause before it is its predicate, but this is weak, because placing the predicate before the subject in such a construction is not permitted.

﴿And Allah is Seeing of what they do﴾, so He will recompense them according to their deeds.

(p-138) ﴿Indeed, they have disbelieved who say, "Indeed, Allah is the Messiah, the son of Mary." And the Messiah said, "O Children of Israel, worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord."﴾ That is: indeed I am a created servant, like you, so worship my Creator and your Creator. ﴿Indeed, whoever associates others with Allah﴾ That is: in His worship, or in what is specific to Him of attributes and acts. ﴿Allah has forbidden him Paradise﴾ He is prevented from entering it, as a forbidden thing is prohibited to one who is forbidden from it, for it is the abode of the monotheists. ﴿And his refuge is the Fire﴾ for it is prepared for the polytheists. ﴿And for the wrongdoers there are no helpers﴾ That is: and for them there is no one who will help them against the Fire. The apparent noun is placed in the position of the pronoun, to record that they wronged themselves by associating others with Allah and turned away from the path of truth. This may be part of the speech of Jesus, peace be upon him, or it may be part of the speech of Allah, the Exalted, alerting by it that they said this exalting Jesus (ﷺ) and seeking nearness to him, while he was opposing them in that and contending with them about it, so what then do you think of others?

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verses 73–74:

﴿Certainly they have disbelieved who say: Indeed, Allah is the third of three.﴾ That is, one of three. This is a report of what the Nestorians (al-Nasturiyyah) and the Melkites (al-Malkaniyyah) among them said, those who hold the doctrine of the three hypostases (al-aqanim al-thalathah). What preceded is the statement of the Jacobites (al-Ya'qubiyyah), who hold the doctrine of union (al-ittihad). ﴿And there is no god except one God.﴾ In existence there is no necessarily existent being deserving of worship, insofar as it is the originator of all existent things, except one God, characterized by oneness (al-wahdaniyyah), exalted above accepting any partner. The word "min" (from) here is extra (mazidah), for the sake of comprehensiveness (li-l-istighraq). ﴿And if they do not desist from what they say,﴾ and do not affirm the oneness of God. ﴿a painful punishment will surely afflict those among them who have disbelieved.﴾ That is, a painful punishment will surely afflict those among them who remained upon disbelief, or the Christians who disbelieved. He placed this in the position of "it will surely afflict them," as a repetition of the testimony to their disbelief and as an alert that the punishment is for whoever persists in disbelief and does not depart from it. Therefore he followed it with his saying: ﴿Will they not repent to Allah and seek His forgiveness?﴾ That is, will they not repent by desisting from those deviant beliefs and statements, and seek His forgiveness by affirming His oneness and His transcendence above union (al-ittihad) and indwelling (al-hulul), after this affirmation and warning. ﴿And Allah is Forgiving and Merciful.﴾ He forgives them and bestows upon them of His bounty if they repent. In this interrogation there is an expression of wonder at their persistence.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 75:

﴿The Messiah, son of Mary, was but a messenger; messengers had passed away before him.﴾ That is: he is nothing but a messenger, like the messengers before him. Allah, glorified and exalted be He, gave him signs (ayat) just as He gave them signs. For the raising of the dead at his hand is (a sign) that He also made the staff (al-'asa) live and become a serpent moving (tas'a) at the hand of Musa, peace be upon him, and that is more wondrous. And if He created him without a father, then He created Adam without a father and a mother, and that is more extraordinary. ﴿And his mother was a truthful woman﴾ like the rest of the women who are constant in truthfulness, or who affirm (yasduqna) the prophets, peace and blessings be upon them. ﴿They both used to eat food﴾ and be in need of it in the manner of animals. He first stated the utmost perfection they had, and indicated that it does not entail divinity for them, because many people share them in the like of it. Then he drew attention to their deficiency and mentioned what contradicts lordship (al-ruburiyya) and requires that they be among the ranks of composite, corruptible created beings. Then he marvelled at those who claim lordship for them despite such clear proofs, so he said:

﴿Look how We make the signs clear to them; then look how they are turned away.﴾ That is, how they are diverted from hearing the truth and reflecting upon it. And "then" (thumma) is used to indicate the difference between the two wonders: that is, Our making the signs clear is a wonder, and their turning away from them is more wondrous.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 76:

﴿Say: Do you worship besides Allah that which possesses neither harm nor benefit for you?﴾ It means ʿĪsā (ʿalayhi al-salām, peace be upon him). Although he possesses that (power) by Allah's granting it to him, glorified and exalted is He, he does not possess it from his own essence, nor does he possess the like of what Allah, exalted is He, inflicts by way of calamities and afflictions, or what He bestows by way of health and abundance. He said "ma" (that which) in view of what he is in his own essence, as a preparation for negating power from him altogether, and as an alert that he belongs to this category; and whoever has a reality that accepts being of the same kind and being a partner is far removed from divinity. He placed harm first because guarding against it is more important than seeking benefit. ﴿And Allah is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾ of the words and the beliefs, so He will recompense for them: if good, then good; and if evil, then evil.

Say: "O People of the Scripture, do not commit excess in your religion beyond the truth" (ghayr al-haqq), that is, excess that is false, by elevating Jesus, peace be upon him, to the point of claiming for him divinity, or by debasing him, claiming that he was of illegitimate birth. It has been said that the address is to the Christians specifically.

"And do not follow the desires of a people who had gone astray before, and led many astray, and went astray from the right way." He means their predecessors and their leaders who had gone astray before the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ) in their own law.

"And led many astray" refers to those who followed them in their innovations and their misguidance. "And went astray from the right way" means from the straight path, which is Islam after his mission (ﷺ), since they denied him and transgressed against him. It has been said that the first (going astray) refers to their going astray from the requirement of reason, and the second refers to their going astray from what the Sharia brought.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verses 78–79:

﴿Those among the Children of Israel who disbelieved were cursed upon the tongue of Dawud (David) and Isa (Jesus) son of Maryam.﴾ That is, Allah cursed them in the Zabur (Psalms) and the Injil (Gospel) through the tongues of those two. It is said that when the people of Ayla (Eilat) transgressed on the Sabbath, Allah the Exalted cursed them upon the tongue of Dawud, and Allah transformed them into apes. And the companions of the table spread (al-ma'ida), when they disbelieved, Isa, upon him be peace, invoked against them and cursed them, and they became swine, and they were five thousand men. ﴿That is because they disobeyed and used to transgress.﴾ That is, that severe curse which necessitated the transformation was on account of their disobedience and their transgression by what was forbidden to them.

﴿They did not forbid one another from any wrong they committed.﴾ That is, they did not forbid one another from repeating a wrong they had committed, or from the like of a wrong they had committed, or from a wrong they intended to do and prepared for; or, they did not desist from it, from their saying "tanahaa 'an al-amr" and "intaha 'anhu" when one refrains. ﴿Evil indeed was what they used to do.﴾ This is an expression of wonder at the badness of their conduct, emphasized by an oath.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 80–81:

﴿You see many of them﴾ from among the People of the Book. ﴿taking as allies those who disbelieve﴾ they take the polytheists as allies out of hatred for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and the believers. ﴿Evil is what their souls have put forward for them﴾ i.e., evil is the thing they have sent ahead, to find it (waiting for them) on the Day of Resurrection, ﴿that Allah has become wrathful toward them, and in the punishment they will abide forever﴾. It is the one singled out for censure, and the meaning is that it necessitates the wrath of Allah and abiding forever in punishment. Or it is the cause of the censure, and the one singled out is omitted, meaning: evil is the thing that that is, because it earned them wrath and eternal abiding.

﴿And if they had believed in Allah and the Prophet﴾ meaning their own Prophet; and although the verse concerns the hypocrites, the intended one is our Prophet, upon him peace. ﴿and in what was sent down to him, they would not have taken them as allies﴾ since faith prevents that. ﴿But many of them are defiantly disobedient﴾ departing from their religion, or persisting obstinately in their hypocrisy.(p-140)

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 82:

﴿You will surely find the most intense of people in enmity toward the believers to be the Jews and those who associate partners with God﴾ due to the severity of their obstinacy, the multiplying of their disbelief, their immersion in following their desires, their reliance on blind imitation (taqlid) and their distance from verification (tahqiq), and their habituation to denying the prophets and opposing them. ﴿And you will surely find the nearest of them in affection toward the believers to be those who say, "We are Christians"﴾ due to the gentleness of their disposition, the softness of their hearts, their small concern for worldly things, and their great attention to knowledge and action. To this He alluded with His saying: ﴿That is because among them are priests and monks, and because they are not arrogant﴾ toward accepting the truth when they understand it, or they are humble and do not behave arrogantly, unlike the Jews. In this is evidence that humility, devotion to knowledge and action, and turning away from base desires are praiseworthy, even if they come from a disbeliever.

And when they hear what has been sent down to the Messenger, you see their eyes overflowing with tears because of the truth they have recognized. It is a continuation (ʿaṭf) of "they are not arrogant" (lā yastakbirūn), and it explains the tenderness of their hearts, the intensity of their fear, their haste to accept the truth, and their lack of resistance to it. Al-fayḍ (overflowing) is the pouring out from fullness, so it is used in place of fullness for emphasis. Or, because of the excess of weeping, their eyes are made to appear as though they overflow of their own accord.

"Because of the truth they have recognized": the first min (mimmā) is for the beginning (ibtidāʾ, i.e., the source), and the second min is for clarifying what they recognized. Or it is for partition (tabʿīḍ), meaning that it is only part of the truth. The meaning is that they recognized some of the truth, and it moved them to tears; so how much more so when they recognize all of it.

They say: "Our Lord, we have believed in this," or "in Muḥammad." ﴿So write us down among the witnesses﴾, that is, among those who testify that it is the truth, or to his prophethood, or among his community, who are witnesses over the nations on the Day of Resurrection.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (*Anwar al-Tanzil*) on surah 5, verse 84:

﴿Why should we not believe in God and in what has come to us of the truth, while we hope that our Lord will admit us along with the righteous people?﴾ This is an *istifham inkar* (interrogation expressing denial, a rhetorical question of disapproval) and *istib'ad* (expressing that something is far-fetched), denying that there is any reason for not believing while the summons is present, namely the hope of being joined with the righteous and entering their company. Alternatively, it is an answer to a questioner who said, "Why did you believe?" The phrase *wa-la nu'minu* is a *hal* (circumstantial clause) from the pronoun, and its *'amil* (governing element) is what is contained in the *lam* of meaning of a verb, meaning: "What has happened to us that we should not believe in God?" That is, not believing in His *wahdaniyya* (oneness), since they were trinitarians. Or [it means not believing] in His Book and His Messenger, for believing in these two is in reality believing in Him; He mentioned them as a preparation and as an exaltation. *Wa-natma'u* is conjoined (*'utifa*) to *nu'minu*, or it is the predicate of an omitted subject, and the *waw* is for the circumstantial clause, meaning: "while we hope." Its governing element is the governing element of the first verb, restricted by it, or *nu'minu*.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verses 85–86:

﴿So Allah rewarded them for what they said﴾, meaning: out of conviction in your statement, "this is the belief of so-and-so," i.e., his creed. ﴿Gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein; and that is the recompense of the doers of good﴾. Those who perfected their reflection and their deeds, or those who habitually did good in matters. And the four verses.

It is narrated: "(It was revealed concerning the Negus (al-Najashi) and his companions. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent to him his letter, and he read it. Then he summoned Ja'far ibn Abi Talib and the emigrants with him, and he brought in the monks and the priests. He commanded Ja'far to recite the Qur'an to them, and he recited Surah Maryam. They wept and believed in the Qur'an.)"

It is also said that it was revealed concerning thirty or seventy men from his people who came as a delegation to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he recited to them Surah Ya-Sin, and they wept and believed.

(p-141) ﴿And those who disbelieved and denied Our signs, those are the companions of the Hellfire﴾. He conjoined denial of the signs of Allah to disbelief, and this is a kind of it, because the purpose is to explain the state of the deniers and to mention them in the context of those who affirm these signs, combining encouragement and warning.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verses 85–86:

﴿So Allah rewarded them for what they said﴾, meaning: out of conviction in your statement, "this is the belief of so-and-so," i.e., his creed. ﴿Gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein; and that is the recompense of the doers of good﴾. Those who perfected their reflection and their deeds, or those who habitually did good in matters. And the four verses.

It is narrated: "(It was revealed concerning the Negus (al-Najashi) and his companions. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent to him his letter, and he read it. Then he summoned Ja'far ibn Abi Talib and the emigrants with him, and he brought in the monks and the priests. He commanded Ja'far to recite the Qur'an to them, and he recited Surah Maryam. They wept and believed in the Qur'an.)"

It is also said that it was revealed concerning thirty or seventy men from his people who came as a delegation to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and he recited to them Surah Ya-Sin, and they wept and believed.
