Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verses 87–88:

﴿O you who believe, do not forbid the good things that Allah has made lawful for you﴾. That is, what is pure and pleasant of them. It is as if, when the preceding verses included praise of the Christians for their monasticism and the exhortation to subdue the self and reject desires, He followed this with a prohibition against excess in that and against transgressing the limits Allah, glorified and exalted is He, has set, by making the lawful unlawful. So He said: ﴿And do not transgress. Indeed, Allah does not love the transgressors﴾. It is also permissible that what is meant is: "Do not transgress the bounds of what Allah has made lawful for you by going over to what He has forbidden to you." Thus the verse forbids both the forbidding of what He has made lawful and the making lawful of what He has forbidden, and calls to moderation between the two.

It is narrated that "the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) once described the Resurrection to his Companions and exaggerated in warning them. They were moved and gathered in the house of Uthman ibn Maz'un, and they agreed that they would not cease to fast and to stand in prayer, that they would not sleep on beds, that they would not eat meat or fat, that they would not approach women or perfume, that they would renounce the world, wear hair-cloth, wander through the earth, and castrate themselves. When this reached the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he said to them: 'I was not commanded with that. Indeed, your selves have a right over you. So fast and break your fast, stand in prayer and sleep, for I stand in prayer and sleep, I fast and break my fast, I eat meat and fat, and I approach women. Whoever turns away from my Sunnah is not of me.' Then this was revealed."

﴿And eat of what Allah has provided for you, lawful and good﴾. That is, eat what is lawful for you and good of what Allah has provided for you. Thus ﹛ḥalālan﹜ is the object (maf'ul) of "eat", and ﹛mimmā﹜ is a circumstantial qualifier (ḥāl) of it that has been placed before it, because the word it qualifies is indefinite (nakirah). It is also permissible for ﹛min﹜ to be inceptive (ibtida'iyyah), connected to "eat". It is also permissible for it to be the object, with ﹛ḥalālan﹜ being a circumstantial qualifier of the relative pronoun or of the omitted returning pronoun, or a qualifier (ṣifah) of an omitted verbal noun (maṣdar). Under all these readings, if provision did not refer to what is forbidden, mentioning the lawful would have no additional benefit. ﴿And fear Allah, in whom you are believers﴾.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 89:

﴿Allah will not hold you accountable for the unintentional oaths in your oaths﴾ It is what comes from a person without intention, like a man's saying: "No, by Allah," and "Yes, by Allah." This is the view of al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him. It was also said: it is swearing to what one thinks is so while it is not so. This is the view of Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him. The phrase "in your oaths" is a complement to "will hold you accountable," or to "the unintentional," since it is a verbal noun or a circumstantial modifier of it. ﴿But He will hold you accountable for what you have bound by oaths﴾ for what you have confirmed the oaths upon with intention and resolve. The meaning is: but He will hold you accountable for what you have bound [by oaths] when you break them, or for the breaking of what you have bound, and it was omitted because it is known. Hamza, al-Kisa'i, and Ibn 'Ayyash, on the authority of 'Asim, read "'aqadtum" with the light form, and Ibn 'Amir, according to the narration of Ibn Dhakwan, read "'aqadtum" (ʿāqadtum), which is from the pattern fa'ala with the meaning of fa'ala. ﴿Then its expiation﴾ then the expiation of its breaking, i.e., the act that removes its sin and covers it. The apparent wording has been used as evidence for the permissibility of expiating with wealth before breaking the oath, and this is contrary to the Hanafis according to us.

Because of the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "Whoever swears to an oath and then sees something else as better than it, let him expiate for his oath and let him do what is better."

﴿Feeding ten needy persons from the middle [standard] of what you feed your families﴾ from the most moderate of it in kind or quantity. It is a mudd for each needy person according to us, and half a sa' according to the Hanafis. Its place in i'rab is the accusative, because it is an attribute of an omitted object, its estimate being: that you feed ten needy persons food from the middle of what you feed. Or it is in the nominative, as a substitute for "feeding." "Ahlun" (families) is like "ardun" (lands) [in its plural pattern]. It was also read "ahaliykum" with the sukun on the ya', according to the dialect of those who make it quiescent in all three cases, like the alif. It is the plural of "ahl," like "al-layali" as the plural of "layl," and "al-aradi" as the plural of "ard." (p-142) It was also said that it is the plural of "ahlah." ﴿Or clothing them﴾ it is conjoined to "feeding," or to "from the middle" if it is taken as a substitute. It is a garment that covers the private parts. It was also said: a comprehensive garment, such as a shirt, a cloak, or a wrapper. It was read with a damma on the kaf, which is a dialect form like qudwa and qudwa, and ka-'usvatihim, meaning the same. Or like what you feed your families, whether extravagantly or sparingly, by which you provide for them, if you do not feed them the middle [standard]. The kaf is in the nominative position, and its estimate is: or feeding them is like their model [the feeding you give yourselves]. ﴿Or freeing a neck﴾ or freeing a human being. Al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with him, stipulated this for oaths by analogy with the expiation for killing. The meaning of "or" is the obligation of one of the three options absolutely, and the choice of the obligated person in determining it. ﴿But whoever does not find [any of these]﴾ i.e., one of them. ﴿Then fasting three days﴾ then its expiation is fasting three days. Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, required that it be consecutive, because it was read "three days consecutively." Anomalous readings are not authoritative according to us when they are not established as Scripture and have not been transmitted as Sunnah. ﴿That﴾ i.e., the aforementioned. ﴿Is the expiation of your oaths when you swear﴾ and break them. ﴿And guard your oaths﴾ by being stingy with them and not spending them on every matter, or by fulfilling them as far as you can without losing good by them, or by expiating them when you break them.

﴿Thus﴾ i.e., like that clarification. ﴿Allah makes clear to you His verses﴾ the signs of His laws. ﴿That perhaps you may be grateful﴾ for the blessing of instruction, or for the blessing of the obligation whose thanks is due, for such clarification makes the way out of it easy for you.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 90:

﴿O you who have believed, indeed, intoxicants, gambling, idolatrous altars, and divining arrows are but defilement from the work of Satan, so avoid it that you may be successful.﴾ That is, the idols (al-asnam) that were set up for worship. ﴿And divining arrows﴾ its explanation has already passed at the beginning of the surah. ﴿Defilement﴾ is filth from which the intellects recoil. He used the singular for it because it is the predicate of "intoxicants" (al-khamr), and the predicate of the conjoined items is omitted, or it is for an omitted noun that is governed, as if he had said: "Indeed, the indulgence in intoxicants and gambling..." ﴿From the work of Satan﴾ because it is caused by his enticement and embellishment. ﴿So avoid it﴾ the pronoun refers to "defilement," or to what has been mentioned, or to "indulgence." ﴿That you may be successful﴾ so that you may succeed by avoiding it.

Know that He, glorified and exalted, emphasized the prohibition of intoxicants and gambling in this verse, by opening the sentence with "indeed" (innama), by linking them with the idolatrous altars and divining arrows, by calling them defilement, and by making them from the work of Satan, as a warning that occupation with them is pure evil or predominantly evil. He commanded avoidance of their very substance and made it a means by which success is hoped for. Then He confirmed this by explaining the worldly and religious corruptions in them that necessitate their prohibition, saying, exalted is He:

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verses 91–92:

﴿Satan only wishes to cause enmity and hatred to arise among you through wine and gambling, and to avert you from the remembrance of Allah and from the prayer﴾. He singled out these two for repeated mention and for explanation of the harm in them, as an alert that they are the principal object of the clarification. He mentioned the stone idols (ansab) and the divining arrows (azlam) to indicate that these two are like them in prohibition and evil.

This is due to His statement, upon him be blessings and peace (ﷺ): "The drinker of wine is like the worshipper of an idol."

He singled out the prayer from among the remembrances by mentioning it separately, to glorify it and to convey that one who turns people away from it is like one who turns people away from faith, since it is its pillar and the distinguishing mark between it and disbelief. Then He repeated the exhortation to desist in the form of a question, arranged upon the types of deterrents mentioned before, saying: ﴿So will you not desist?﴾ This indicates that the matter of prohibition and warning has reached its utmost limit and that excuses have been cut off.

﴿And obey Allah and obey the Messenger﴾ in what they command. ﴿And beware﴾ of what they forbid, or of opposing them. ﴿But if you turn away, then know that the duty of Our Messenger is only the clear conveyance﴾. That is: know that you have not harmed the Messenger (ﷺ) by your turning away, for upon him is only the conveyance, and he has fulfilled it; rather, you have harmed only yourselves by it.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 93:

﴿There is no blame upon those who believe and do righteous deeds for what they have eaten﴾ of what was not forbidden to them, due to His saying: ﴿when they fear [Allah], and believe, and do righteous deeds﴾, meaning: they avoid what is forbidden and remain steadfast in faith and in righteous deeds. ﴿Then fear [Allah]﴾ regarding what was subsequently forbidden to them, such as wine. ﴿And believe﴾ in its prohibition. ﴿Then fear [Allah]﴾, then they persist and remain steadfast in avoiding sins. ﴿And do good﴾, and they seek out beautiful deeds and occupy themselves with them.

It is related that: "When the prohibition of wine was revealed, the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, said: 'O Messenger of Allah, what about our brothers who died while they were drinking wine and eating gambling gains?' Then this was revealed."

It is possible that this repetition is in reference to the three times, or in reference to the three states of a person's use of taqwa (God-consciousness) and faith: between himself and himself, between himself and people, and between himself and Allah the Exalted. For this reason, he replaced "faith" with "good" in the third repetition, pointing to what the Prophet (ﷺ) said in explaining it. Or it may refer to the three stages: the beginning, the middle, and the end. Or it may refer to what one guards against: one should abandon the prohibited things to avoid punishment, doubtful matters to guard against falling into the forbidden, and some permissible things to preserve the self from baseness and to refine it from the defilement of nature. ﴿And Allah loves the good-doers﴾, so He does not hold them accountable for anything. In this is the indication that whoever does this becomes a good-doer, and whoever becomes a good-doer becomes beloved to Allah.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 94:

﴿O you who have believed, Allah will surely test you with [some] game which your hands and spears can reach﴾ It was revealed concerning the year of al-Hudaybiyah. Allah, glorified and exalted be He, tested them with game, and wild animals would come upon them in their encampments such that they could hunt them, by seizing them with their hands and stabbing them with their spears, while they were in the state of ihram (sacred state of pilgrimage). The diminishing and belittling expressed by "with [some]" serves to alert that it is not among the great trials that cause feet to slip, such as being tested by the sacrifice of souls and wealth. Whoever does not remain steadfast in this, how will he remain steadfast in what is greater than it?

﴿That Allah may make evident who fears Him in the unseen﴾ so that the one who fears His punishment while unseen, awaiting it, is distinguished, owing to the strength of his faith, from the one who does not fear Him, owing to the weakness of his heart and the scarcity of his faith. He mentioned "knowing" but intended the occurrence and manifestation of the known, or the attachment of knowledge (to the object).

﴿And whoever transgresses after that﴾ after that trial with game.

﴿For him is a painful punishment﴾ The threat applies to him. For whoever cannot master his composure in such a matter and does not observe Allah's ruling concerning it, then how about him in what the soul is more inclined to and more eager for?

O you who have believed, do not kill game while you are in the state of ihram (ihram, the sacred state of pilgrimage). ﴿أيْ مُحْرِمُونَ﴾ i.e., while you are muhrimun (those in ihram). It is the plural of haram, like radah and rudah. Perhaps he mentioned "killing" rather than "slaughtering and sacrificing" for generality. By game he meant what is eaten, since that is what is customarily predominant in it, and the Prophet's saying supports this, may blessings and peace be upon him: "Five creatures may be killed both within the sacred precinct and outside it: the kite, the crow, the scorpion, the mouse, and the rabid dog." In another narration, "the snake" replaces "the scorpion," along with an indication of the permissibility of killing every harmful creature. It is disputed whether this prohibition nullifies the ruling on slaughter, so that the slaughtered animal of one in ihram is treated like carrion and the slaughtered animal of a polytheist, or does not, so that it is like a shared sheep when the usurper slaughters it.

﴿وَمَن قَتَلَهُ مِنكم مُتَعَمِّدًا﴾ remembering his ihram and knowing that it is forbidden for him before he kills it. Most scholars hold that his mention of this is not to restrict the obligation of compensation, since the destruction of game by one who acts intentionally and one who acts in error is the same in requiring compensation. Rather, it is for His saying: ﴿وَمَن عادَ فَيَنْتَقِمُ اللَّهُ مِنهُ﴾ (and whoever returns, Allah will take retribution from him). Also, the verse was revealed concerning one who acted intentionally, since it is narrated that during the 'Umrah of al-Hudaybiyah a wild donkey appeared to them, and Abu al-Yusr struck it with his spear and killed it. Then the verse was revealed.

﴿فَجَزاءٌ مِثْلُ ما قَتَلَ مِنَ النَّعَمِ﴾ (then a compensation equal to what he killed of the livestock), with jaza' in the nominative. The reading of "mithl" is that of the Kufans and Ya'qub, in the sense of fa-'alayhi (so it is incumbent upon him), i.e., so it is incumbent upon him a compensation that is equivalent to what he killed of the livestock. On this reading the prepositional phrase does not attach to jaza', because of the separation between them by the qualifier, since the complement of a verbal noun functions like its relative clause, so it is not described before it is completed; rather, it is its qualifier. The rest read it with the verbal noun added to its object, and "mithl" is inserted as in their saying "mithli la yaqulu kadha" (someone like me does not say such a thing), and the meaning is: it is incumbent upon him that he be made to give the equivalent of what he killed. It was also read as "fa-jaza'an mithla ma qatala" with both in the accusative, meaning: then let him give a compensation, or: it is incumbent upon him to give a compensation equivalent to what he killed, and his compensation is the equivalent of what he killed. This equivalence is in terms of form and appearance according to Malik and al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with them both, while according to Abu Hanifah, may Allah have mercy on him, it is value. He said: the game is valued where it was hunted; if the value reaches the price of a sacrificial animal, one may choose between sacrificing an animal whose value equals it, or buying food with it and giving each poor person half a sa' of wheat or a sa' of something else, or fasting one day for the food of each poor person. If the value does not reach that, one may choose between feeding and fasting. The wording of the first is more appropriate.

﴿يَحْكُمُ بِهِ ذَوا عَدْلٍ مِنكُمْ﴾ (judged by two just men among you) is a qualifier of jaza'. It may also be a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun in its predicate or from it if you make it an annexed noun, or if you make it a qualifier and raise it with an implied predicate for "man." Just as valuation requires examination and effort, so too it requires equivalence in form and appearance to it, since species resemble one another greatly.

It is also read "dhu 'adl" (one just man), intending the category or the imam. ﴿هَدْيًا﴾ (as an offering) is a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "bihi" or from jaza', even if it is nunated because it is specified by the qualifier; or it is an apposition to "mithl" in terms of its position or its wording for whoever put it in the accusative. ﴿بالِغَ الكَعْبَةِ﴾ (reaching the Ka'bah) is a qualifier of hadyan, because its annexation is verbal; the meaning of its reaching the Ka'bah is slaughtering it in the Haram and giving it in charity. Abu Hanifah said: he slaughters it in the Haram and gives it in charity wherever he wishes. ﴿أوْ كَفّارَةٌ﴾ (or an expiation) is conjoined to jaza' if you raise it, and if you put it in the accusative, then it is the predicate of an elided subject. ﴿طَعامُ مَساكِينَ﴾ (feeding of the poor) is an explanatory apposition or an apposition to it, or the predicate of an elided subject, i.e., it is food. Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read "kaffaratun ta'amu" with the annexation for specification, as in your saying "khatamun fiddatin" (a ring of silver). The meaning according to al-Shafi'i is that he expiates by feeding the poor an amount equal in value to the sacrificial animal from the staple food of the land, giving each poor person a mudd. ﴿أوْ عَدْلُ ذَلِكَ صِيامًا﴾ (or its equivalent in fasting), or whatever equals it of fasting, so he fasts one day for the food of each poor person. It is originally a verbal noun used for the object. It was also read with a kasra on the 'ayn, which is what is equal to a thing in measure, like the two equal loads of a burden. "Dhalika" refers to the food, and "siyaman" is a specification for "'adl." ﴿لِيَذُوقَ وبالَ أمْرِهِ﴾ (that he may taste the consequence of his deed) is connected to an elided element, i.e., then upon him is the compensation, or the food, or the fasting, so that he may taste the burden of his action and the evil outcome of violating the sanctity of ihram; or the severe burden of opposing the command of Allah Most High. The root of "wabal" is heaviness, and from it comes "ta'am wabil" (a heavy food). ﴿عَفا اللَّهُ عَمّا سَلَفَ﴾ (Allah has pardoned what has passed) refers to killing game while in ihram in the Jahiliyyah, or before the prohibition, or in this instance. ﴿وَمَن عادَ﴾ (and whoever returns) to the like of this. ﴿فَيَنْتَقِمُ اللَّهُ مِنهُ﴾ (then Allah will take retribution from him), i.e., He takes retribution from him, and there is nothing in it that prevents expiation for the one who returns, as is reported from Ibn 'Abbas and Shurayh. ﴿واللَّهُ عَزِيزٌ ذُو انْتِقامٍ﴾ (And Allah is Mighty, Possessor of retribution) against those who persist in disobeying Him.

﴿Lawful for you is the game of the sea﴾: this means what is caught from it, of that which lives only in water, and all of it is lawful, based on the Prophet's saying (ﷺ) about the sea: "Its water is pure, and its dead creatures are lawful." 

Abu Hanifa said: only fish is lawful from it. It was also said: fish and whatever its counterpart on land is eaten are lawful. Its "provision" (ṭaʿām) is what the sea casts up or what recedes from it. It was also said: the pronoun refers to the game, and its "provision" (ṭaʿām) is its eating. ﴿A provision for you﴾: an enjoyment for you, put in the accusative (manṣūb) as an object of purpose (maf'ūl li-ajlihi). ﴿And for the travelers﴾: that is, for your travelers, who take it along as dried provisions (qadīd). 

﴿But the game of the land is forbidden to you﴾: that is, what is caught in it, or hunting in it. According to the first meaning, what is caught by a non-pilgrim is also forbidden to the one in the state of ihram (muḥrim), even if he had no part in catching it. The majority hold it lawful, based on the Prophet's saying (ﷺ): "The meat of game is lawful for you, as long as you do not hunt it yourselves or have it hunted for you." (p-145)

﴿As long as you are in the state of ḥurum﴾: that is, in the state of ihram (muḥrimīn). It is also read as "dimtum" with a kasra on the dal, from the verb dāma yadāmu (to last).

﴿And fear God, to whom you will be gathered﴾.

﴿Allah has made the Ka'bah﴾ — He appointed it. The House was named "Ka'bah" because of its cubical shape (takaʿʿub). ﴿the Sacred House﴾ is either an explicative apposition (ʿatf bayān) by way of praise, or the second object. ﴿as a means of support for the people﴾ — i.e., the cause of their being sustained in matters of their livelihood and their hereafter: the fearful take refuge in it, the weak find security in it, merchants profit through it, and pilgrims and visitors (ʿumrah performers) turn toward it. Alternatively, it means that through it the affairs of their religion and their worldly life are upheld. Ibn ʿĀmir read ﴿qiyaman﴾ as "qiyaman," taking it to be a verbal noun of the pattern fiʿal, like shibaʿ (satiety), whose middle radical was made weak as happened in its verb; its accusative case is either as a verbal noun (maṣdar) or as a circumstantial state (ḥāl). ﴿and the sacred month, and the offerings, and the garlands﴾ — their explanation has already preceded. The "sacred month" is the month in which the Hajj is performed, namely Dhu al-Hijjah, because it is the one suitable to its companions (the months mentioned with it); it is also said that it refers to the category (of sacred months). ﴿That﴾ refers either to the making (of the Ka'bah and these institutions) or to what was mentioned of the command to preserve the sanctity of the state of ihram and other things. ﴿So that you may know that Allah knows what is in the heavens and what is in the earth﴾ — for the legislation of rulings to ward off harms before they occur and to bring about the benefits that follow from them is evidence of the wisdom of the Lawgiver and the perfection of His knowledge. ﴿And that Allah is All-Knowing of everything﴾ — a generalization after a specification, and an emphasis after an absolute statement.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verses 98–99:

﴿Know that Allah is severe in punishment, and that Allah is Forgiving and Merciful﴾. This is a warning and a promise for those who violate His sacred prohibitions, and for those who observe them; or for those who persist in them, and for those who abandon them.

﴿The Messenger's duty is only to convey (the message)﴾. This is an emphasis on the obligation to carry out what he was commanded to do; that is, the Messenger has done what he was commanded to do, which is to convey (the message), and you have no excuse left for neglect. ﴿And Allah knows what you disclose and what you conceal﴾, of belief and disbelief, of deed and intention.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 100:

﴿Say: Not equal are the bad and the good.﴾ This is a general ruling affirming that there is no equality in the sight of God, glorified and exalted be He, between the inferior among persons, deeds and wealth and their superior. He encourages, through it, what is good in deeds and lawful in wealth. ﴿And even if the abundance of the bad should impress you﴾ — for the consideration is with quality and inferiority, not with scarcity and abundance, since the praiseworthy few is better than the blameworthy many. The address is to everyone who takes heed, and for this reason He said: ﴿So be mindful of God, O people of understanding﴾, meaning: be mindful of Him in seeking out the bad even if it is abundant, and prefer the good even if it is little. ﴿That you may succeed﴾, hoping that you may attain success.

It is narrated that it was revealed concerning the pilgrims of al-Yamamah when the Muslims intended to attack them, and they were forbidden from doing so, even though they were polytheists.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verses 101–102:

﴿O you who believe, do not ask about things which, if they were made known to you, would distress you; but if you ask about them while the Qur'an is being revealed, they will be made known to you.﴾ The conditional clause (al-shart̲iyyah) and what is conjoined to it are two descriptive clauses (ṣifatān) for "things" (ashyā'). The meaning is: Do not ask the Messenger of God (ﷺ) about things which, if they were to become manifest to you, would grieve you; and if you ask about them in the time of revelation, they will become manifest to you. These two, like two premises (muqaddimatān), produce a conclusion that prevents the asking, namely that it is among the things that grieve them, and the intelligent person does not do what grieves him.

"Ashyā'" is a collective noun (ism jam') like ṭarfā' (tamarisk), except that its final radical was transposed, so it became lafā'. It was also said that it is af'ilā' (pattern), whose final radical was deleted, being the plural of shay', on the basis that its origin is shayyi' like hayyin, or shay' like ṣadīq, which was lightened. It was also said that it is af'āl, the plural of shay' without any change, like bayt and abyāt; but its being diptote (mamnū' min al-ṣarf) refutes this.

﴿God has pardoned you for them﴾ is another descriptive clause, i.e., about things from which God has pardoned, and about which He did not impose obligations. For it is narrated that when the verse ﴿And for God, upon mankind, is the pilgrimage to the House﴾ was revealed, Suraqah ibn Malik said: "Is it every year?" The Messenger of God (ﷺ) turned away from him until he repeated it three times. He said: "No. Had I said yes, it would have become obligatory, and had it become obligatory, you would not have been able to do it. So leave me as I have left you." Then this verse was revealed.

Or it is a new sentence (isti'nāf), i.e., God has pardoned what has passed of your asking, so do not return to the like of it.

﴿And God is Forgiving, Forbearing﴾: He does not hasten to punish you for what slips from you, and He pardons much. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with them both, that (the Prophet, upon him be prayers and peace, was once delivering a sermon while angry because of the great number of questions they asked about matters that did not concern them. He said: "Ask me about anything and I will answer." A man said: "Where is my father?" He said: "In the Fire." Another said: "Who is my father?" He said: "Hudhafah." He was called by other than his father. Then this verse was revealed.)

﴿Certainly a people before you asked about them﴾: the pronoun refers to the question (al-mas'alah) indicated by "do you ask" (tas'alū), and for this reason it is not governed by "about" ('an) nor is "things" (ashyā') governed with the preposition deleted.

﴿from before you﴾ is connected to "asked" (sa'alahā) and is not a descriptor of "a people," for a temporal adverbial cannot be a descriptor of a substance (juththah), nor a circumstantial clause from it, nor a predicate about it. ﴿Then they became disbelievers in them﴾: i.e., because of them, since they did not comply with what they asked, out of denial.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 103:

﴿Allah has not instituted any bahira, nor sa'iba, nor wasila, nor ham﴾ This is a rejection and denunciation of what the people of the Jahiliyya (the Age of Ignorance, pre-Islamic period) had innovated. Their practice was that when a she-camel gave birth to five young, the last of which was a male, they would slit (bahharu) her ear, that is, split it, and leave her free (khallaw sabilaha), so she was not ridden and not milked. A man among them would say: "If I am cured, my she-camel is a sa'iba," and he would treat her like the bahira in forbidding any benefit from her. And when a ewe gave birth to a female, it belonged to them; if it gave birth to a male, it was for their gods; and if it gave birth to both, they said the female had joined (wasalat) her brother, so the male was not slaughtered for them. And when a stallion sired ten offspring, they forbade its back (hamaw zahrahu), did not prevent it from water or pasture, and said: "Its back has been protected (qad hamiya zahruhu)." The meaning of "jaʿala" here is "shara'a wa-waddaʿa" (prescribed and laid down); for this reason it transitively takes one object, which is "al-bahira," and "min" is extra (mazida).

﴿But those who disbelieve invent lies against Allah﴾ by forbidding these things and attributing them to Allah, glory be to Him and exalted.

﴿And most of them do not understand﴾ that is, the lawful from the unlawful and the permitted from the forbidden, or the commanding from the forbidding. But they follow their elders blindly (yuqallidun kibarahum). It is also said that among them are those who know that this is false, but love of leadership and blind imitation of their fathers prevent them from acknowledging it.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 104:

﴿And when it is said to them, "Come to what Allah has sent down and to the Messenger," they say, "Sufficient for us is what we found our fathers upon."﴾ This is a statement of the deficiency of their intellects, their immersion in imitation (taqlid, blind adherence to authority), and that they have no support other than it. ﴿Even though their fathers knew nothing and were not guided?﴾ The wāw is for the circumstantial (ḥāl) and the hamzah (interrogative particle) entered upon it to deny the act in this state. That is, do I suppose them to follow what they found their fathers upon even if the fathers were ignorant and astray? The meaning is that following (iqtida') is valid only with one who is known to be learned and guided, and that is not known except through proof (ḥujjah), so taqlid is not sufficient.

﴿O you who believe, take care of yourselves﴾. That is: preserve them and be steadfast in reforming them. The preposition-with-object phrase (al-jarr ma'a al-majrur) is treated as a noun (ism) for "be steadfast," which is why ﻧَﻔْﺴَﻜُﻢ (anfusakum) is in the accusative. It is also read in the nominative (anfusukum) as a beginning (mubtada').

﴿No harm will come to you from those who have gone astray, if you are guided﴾. That is: misguidance will not harm you if you are rightly guided. Among being guided is that one forbids what is wrong to the extent of one's ability, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever among you sees an evil, let him change it with his hand; if he is unable, then with his tongue; and if he is unable, then with his heart."

The verse was revealed when the believers were grieving over the disbelievers and wishing for their faith. It is also said that when a man embraced Islam, they would say to him, "You have foolished your fathers," and so this was revealed. ﴿No harm will come to you﴾ (lā yaḍurrukum) may be read in the nominative as a resumptive sentence (mustaʾnif), and this is supported by the reading "lā yaḍīrukum." It may be read in the jussive as a response (jawāb) or as a prohibition (nahy), but the rāʾ is then given a ḍamma by way of ittibāʿ (harmonization of vowels), since the ḍamma of the ḍād was transferred to it from the rāʾ that was assimilated (idghām). This is supported by the reading of one who read "lā yaḍarrukum" with a fatḥa, and "lā yuḍirrukum" with a kasra or ḍamma on the ḍād, from ḍārrahu, yaḍīruhu and yaḍūruhu.

﴿To God you will all return, and He will inform you of what you used to do﴾. This is a promise and a warning to both groups, and an admonition that no one is held accountable for another's sin.

O you who believe, the testimony between you (means) — that is, regarding what you have been commanded — is that of two witnesses among you. The word "testimony" here means calling witnesses to a bequest, and its being attributed to the time (shahadatu baynikum) is an extended usage. It is also read as shahādatan with the accusative and tanwin, governed by "li-yuqim" (let him establish). ﴿When death approaches one of you﴾ — that is, when it draws near and its signs appear — and this is a time-clause related to the testimony. ﴿At the time of bequest﴾ is a substitute (badal) for it; and in using it as a substitute there is an alert that bequest is something not to be taken lightly; or it is an adverbial complement of "approaches" (hadara). ﴿Two﴾ is the subject (fa'il) of "testimony", and it may also be its predicate (khabar) with an elided genitive (mudaf).

﴿Two men of justice from among you﴾ — that is, from among your kin, or from among the Muslims; and these two are attributes of "two". ﴿Or two others from outside your group﴾ is conjoined to "two". Whoever interprets "others" (al-ghayr) as the People of the Covenant (ahl al-dhimmah) takes it as abrogated, since their testimony against a Muslim is, by consensus (ijma'), not accepted. ﴿If you travel in the land﴾ — that is, you journey through it. ﴿And the calamity of death befalls you﴾ — that is, you approach the term (ajal). ﴿You detain them﴾ — you hold them back and make them wait; this is an attribute of "two others". The condition, together with its elided answer indicated by his saying ﴿or two others from outside your group﴾, is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiradh), its benefit being to show that two of your own should testify, and if this is impossible, as in travel, then from outside your group; or it is a resumptive statement (isti'naf), as if it were said: "What shall we do if we doubt the two witnesses?" and He said: "You detain them."

﴿After the prayer﴾ — the afternoon prayer (salat al-'asr), because it is the time when people gather and the angels of the night and the angels of the day meet. It is also said: any prayer whatever. ﴿They both swear by God, if you doubt﴾ — if the heir among you doubts. ﴿We will not sell it for any price﴾ is the thing sworn to; and "if you doubt" is a parenthetical insertion indicating that the oath is restricted to the state of doubt. The meaning: we will not exchange the oath, or God, for any worldly gain; that is, we will not swear falsely by God out of greed. ﴿Even if he were a near kinsman﴾ — even if the one for whom the oath is made were close to us; its answer is also elided, namely "we will not sell it." ﴿Nor will we conceal the testimony of God﴾ — that is, the testimony which God commanded us to establish. It is reported from al-Sha'bi that he paused at "shahadah" and then began "Allah" with the extended vowel, eliding the particle of oath and compensating with the interrogative particle; and it is reported from him with other readings, like the people's saying "Allahi la-af'alanna." ﴿Then indeed we would be among the sinners﴾ — that is, if we concealed it. It is also read as "lamila'thimin", by eliding the hamza, transferring its vowel to the lam, and assimilating the nun into it.

﴿Then if it is discovered﴾, that is, if it becomes known, ﴿that the two have incurred sin﴾, that is, that they committed an act that brought about sin, such as distortion. ﴿Then two others﴾, that is, two other witnesses, ﴿shall stand in their place from among those against whom﴾ the claim ﴿has been established﴾, that is, from among those who were wronged by them, and they are the heirs. Hafs read "isthaqqa" (has been established) in the active voice (ibni li-l-fa'il), and the subject is ﴿al-awlayan﴾ (the two nearest). ﴿The two nearest﴾ are the two most entitled to testify because of their kinship and their knowledge. This is the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "they are the two nearest," or the predicate of ﴿two others﴾, or the subject of a sentence whose predicate is ﴿two others﴾, or an apposition to them or to the pronoun in ﴿shall stand﴾. Hamza, Ya'qub and Abu Bakr, on the authority of Asim, read "al-awwalin" (the first ones) as an attribute of "alladhina" (those), or as an apposition to it, meaning "from among the first ones who have been wronged." It has also been read "al-awlayn" in the dual, its case being accusative by way of praise, and "al-awwalan" with the same grammatical analysis (i'rab) as "al-awlayan."

﴿So they shall swear by God: "Our testimony is more truthful than their testimony﴾, that is, more truthful than theirs and more deserving of being accepted. ﴿And we have not transgressed﴾, that is, we have not exceeded the truth in it. ﴿Indeed we would then be among the wrongdoers﴾, those who put falsehood in the place of truth, or those who wrong themselves if we had transgressed.

The meaning of the two verses is that when a dying person wishes to make a bequest, it is fitting that he call two just men from among his relatives or from among his religious community to witness his bequest, or that he entrust it to them as a precaution. If he cannot find them, for instance because he is on a journey, then two others from outside them. Then if a dispute and doubt arise, they shall swear to the truth of what they say, with an emphatic oath at the time of the prayer. If it becomes known that they lied, through a sign or strong indication, then two others from among the heirs of the deceased shall swear. The ruling is abrogated (naskh, abrogation) if the two are witnesses, for then it does not require the witness to swear and does not set his oath against the oath of the heir. It remains in force if the two are executors, and the oath is returned to the heirs, either because the treachery of the two executors has become apparent, since the executor is believed by oath because of his trustworthiness, or because the claim has changed.

This is because it is related that Tamim al-Dari and Adi ibn Yazid set out for Syria for trade, and at that time they were Christians, and with them was Budayl, the freedman of Amr ibn al-As, who was a Muslim. When they arrived in Syria, Budayl fell ill, so he wrote down what he had with him in a document and put it among his goods, and did not inform them of it. He appointed them executors, to deliver his goods to his family, and then he died. They searched his property and took from it a silver vessel with three hundred mithqals, decorated with gold, and they concealed it. His family found the document and demanded the vessel from them, but they denied it. So they brought the matter before the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and this verse was revealed: "O you who have believed..." And the Messenger of God (ﷺ) made them swear after the afternoon prayer at the pulpit, and released them. Then the vessel was found in their hands. The Banu Sahm came to them about this, and they said: "We bought it from him, but we had no evidence, so we disliked bringing it forward." So they referred them to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and this verse was revealed: "Then if it is discovered..." Then Amr ibn al-As and al-Muttalib ibn Abi Wada'a of the Banu Sahm stood up, swore, and claimed it.

Perhaps the specifying of the number in these two verses is due to the particular circumstances of this event.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 108:

﴿That﴾, i.e., the ruling previously mentioned, or the swearing of the witness. ﴿is closer to [their] bringing the testimony in its proper form﴾, in the manner in which they bore it, without distortion or betrayal in it. ﴿or they fear that oaths will be returned after their oaths﴾, that the oath will be returned to the claimants after their oaths, so they would be disgraced by the exposure of betrayal and a false oath. He used the plural pronoun because it is a ruling that applies to all the witnesses. ﴿And fear God and listen﴾ to what you are enjoined, listening with acceptance. ﴿And God does not guide the defiant people﴾, i.e., if you do not fear God and do not listen, you will be a defiant people, and God does not guide the defiant people, i.e., does not guide them to proof or to the path of Paradise. Then His saying, exalted is He:

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 109:

﴿On the Day when Allah gathers the Messengers﴾ is an adverbial complement (zarf) governed by a verb implied in what follows. It is also said to be a substitute (badal) for the object of "and fear" (wattaqu), a substitution of part-of-whole type (badal al-ishtimal), or for the object of "and listen" (wasma'u), with an elided noun, meaning "and listen to the news of the Day of their gathering", or it is accusative by an implied "remember" (idhkur).

﴿Then He will say﴾ i.e., to the Messengers.

﴿"What was the response you received?"﴾ i.e., what kind of response you were given, with "madha" in the position of a verbal noun (masdar), or "with what did you respond?", where the preposition is elided. This question is for the rebuke of their people, just as the question put to the buried infant girl (al-mawuda) is for the rebuke of the one who buried her. Therefore ﴿They will say: "We have no knowledge"﴾ i.e., we have no knowledge of what you know.

﴿Indeed, You are the Knower of the unseen﴾, so You know what we know of what they answered us and displayed to us, and what we do not know of what they concealed in their hearts. In this there is a complaint about them and a referral of the matter to His knowledge of what they inflicted upon them. It is also said the meaning is: we have no knowledge in comparison with Your knowledge, or: we have no knowledge of what they introduced after us, and the judgment is only for the final outcome. It is read "'Allam" in the accusative, on the basis that the speech is complete with "Indeed, You are", meaning "Indeed, You are the One described by Your well-known attributes", and "'Allam" is in the accusative by way of specification (al-ikhtisas) or address (al-nida'). Abu Bakr and Hamza read "al-Ghuyub" with a kasra on the ghayn wherever it occurs.(p-149)

﴿When God said, "O Jesus son of Mary, remember My favour upon you and upon your mother"﴾ is a substitution (badal) for "the Day when He gathers," and it follows the same pattern as "and the companions of the Garden will call out." The meaning is that He, glorified and exalted, rebukes the disbelievers on that day by questioning the messengers about how their communities responded to them, and by enumerating the signs He manifested through them. So one group denied the messengers and called them sorcerers, while others went to excess and took them as gods. Or it is in the accusative by an implied "remember" (udhkur).

﴿when I strengthened you﴾, meaning I strengthened you. It is an adverbial of time (zarf) governing "My favour," or a circumstantial clause (hal) from it. It was also read as "āyyadtuka."

﴿with the Holy Spirit﴾: with Gabriel, peace be upon him. Or it means the word by which religion is given life, or the soul, which gives eternal life and purifies from sins. This is supported by His saying: ﴿You speak to people in the cradle and in maturity﴾, that is, existing in the cradle and in maturity. The meaning is that you speak to them in childhood and in old age alike. The meaning is that his state in childhood is placed on a par with his state in maturity, in full reason and speech. From this it has been argued that he will descend, since he was raised up before reaching middle age.

﴿And when I taught you the Book and the Wisdom, and the Torah and the Gospel. And when you shaped from clay as the form of a bird, by My permission, then you breathed into it and it became a bird by My permission, and you healed the blind and the leper by My permission, and when you brought forth the dead by My permission﴾: its explanation has already passed in Surat Al 'Imran. Nafi' and Ya'qub read "ṭā'iran" (a bird), and the word admits both the singular and the plural, like "al-bāqir."

﴿And when I restrained the Children of Israel from you﴾, meaning the Jews, when they resolved to kill him. ﴿When you came to them with clear proofs﴾ is a time clause governing "I restrained." ﴿Those of them who disbelieved said, "This is nothing but evident sorcery"﴾, meaning: what you have brought is nothing but evident sorcery. Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "illā sāḥirun" (except a sorcerer), in which case the reference is to Jesus, peace be upon him.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (*Anwar al-Tanzil*) on surah 5, verses 111–112:

﴿And when I inspired the disciples (al-Ḥawāriyyūn)﴾, i.e., I commanded them through the tongues of My messengers. ﴿To believe in Me and My messenger﴾. It is permissible for أنْ to be a verbal particle (maṣdariyya, "that" introducing a verbal noun) and for أنْ to be explanatory (mufassira). ﴿They said, "We believe, and bear witness that we are Muslims"﴾, meaning sincere (mukhlisūn).

﴿When the disciples said, "O Jesus, son of Mary"﴾: the phrase إذْ is governed in the accusative (manṣūb bi-l-dhikr), meaning it is governed by an implied verb of mentioning, such as "remember." Alternatively, it is an adverb of time (ẓarf) modifying qālū ("they said"). In that case it serves as a reminder that their claim of sincerity was at odds with their words. ﴿Can your Lord send down to us a table from heaven?﴾ This question shows that they had not yet attained firm, well-established knowledge. It is also said that this "ability" (istiṭāʿa) means ability in accordance with what wisdom and will require, not in accordance with mere power. It is also said that the meaning is: "Will your Lord comply (yuṭīʿu)? That is, will He answer you?" Here istaṭāʿa carries the sense of aṭāʿa, just as istajāba and ajāba both mean "to respond." Al-Kisā'ī read ﴿Will your Lord comply (tastaṭīʿu rabbaka)?﴾, meaning: "Will you ask your Lord for that without any hindrance?" The māʾida (table) is the spread (khuwān) when food is on it. It is named from the root m-w-d, as in māda al-māʾu yamīdu ("the water moved") when it shakes, or from māda, meaning "he gave," since it seems to sway (tamīdu) those to whom it is presented. A parallel is the expression shajara muṭʿama ("a fruit-bearing tree"). ﴿He said, "Fear Allah"﴾ from such requests. ﴿If you are believers﴾ in the perfection of His power and the truth of my prophethood, or: "if you are truthful in your claim to faith."

Commentary of al-Baydawi (*Anwar al-Tanzil*) on surah 5, verses 111–112:

﴿And when I inspired the disciples (al-Ḥawāriyyūn)﴾, i.e., I commanded them through the tongues of My messengers. ﴿To believe in Me and My messenger﴾. It is permissible for أنْ to be a verbal particle (maṣdariyya, "that" introducing a verbal noun) and for أنْ to be explanatory (mufassira). ﴿They said, "We believe, and bear witness that we are Muslims"﴾, meaning sincere (mukhlisūn).

﴿When the disciples said, "O Jesus, son of Mary"﴾: the phrase إذْ is governed in the accusative (manṣūb bi-l-dhikr), meaning it is governed by an implied verb of mentioning, such as "remember." Alternatively, it is an adverb of time (ẓarf) modifying qālū ("they said"). In that case it serves as a reminder that their claim of sincerity was at odds with their words. ﴿Can your Lord send down to us a table from heaven?﴾ This question shows that they had not yet attained firm, well-established knowledge. It is also said that this "ability" (istiṭāʿa) means ability in accordance with what wisdom and will require, not in accordance with mere power. It is also said that the meaning is: "Will your Lord comply (yuṭīʿu)? That is, will He answer you?" Here istaṭāʿa carries the sense of aṭāʿa, just as istajāba and ajāba both mean "to respond." (p-150) ﴿They said: "We wish to eat from it"﴾ — a preface to an excuse, and an explanation of what prompted them to ask, namely that they wish to enjoy eating from it.

﴿"And that our hearts may be reassured"﴾ — by the combining of knowledge of direct observation (ʿilm al-mushāhadah) with knowledge by inference (ʿilm al-istidlāl), through the perfection of His power, glory be to Him and exalted is He. ﴿"And that we may know that you have indeed spoken truth to us"﴾ — regarding the claim to prophethood; or that God answers our supplication. ﴿"And that we may be among the witnesses to it"﴾ — if you call us to bear witness, or among the witnesses of what is seen, not merely those who hear a report.

﴿Jesus, son of Mary, said﴾ — when he saw that they had a sound purpose in this, or that they would not desist from it, so he wished to press the proof upon them in its completeness. ﴿"O God, our Lord, send down upon us a table from heaven to be a festival (ʿīd) for us"﴾ — that is, the day of its descending shall be a festival which we honour.

It is said that ʿīd means a recurring joy, and for this reason the day of festivity is called ʿīd. It is also read as "takun" (it shall be), as a response to the imperative. ﴿"For the first of us and the last of us"﴾ — a substitute for "for us," with the governing verb repeated; that is, a festival for those who came before us and those who come after us. It is related that it descended on a Sunday, and for this reason the Christians took it as a festival. It is also said: the first of us and the last of us shall eat from it. It is read as "li-ūlānā wa-ukhrānā," meaning the community or the group. ﴿"And a sign from You"﴾ — conjoined to "a festival." ﴿"from You"﴾ — an attribute of it, that is, a sign coming from You, indicating the perfection of Your power and the soundness of my prophethood. ﴿"And provide for us"﴾ — the table and the thankfulness for it. ﴿"And You are the best of providers"﴾ — that is, the best of those who provide, for He is the Creator of provision and its Giver without recompense.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verse 115:

﴿Allah said: "Indeed I will send it down to you"﴾, in response to your request. Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and 'Asim recited *munazziluhā* with the doubled *zay* (*bi-l-tashdid*).

﴿So whoever among you disbelieves after that, I will surely punish him with a punishment﴾, i.e., a punishment (*ta'dhīban*, the verbal noun). It is also permissible to treat *'adhāban* as a direct object (*maf'ūl bihi*) by way of extension (*'alā al-si'a*). ﴿I will not punish him﴾: the pronoun refers to the verbal noun (*al-maṣdar*), or to *al-'adhāb* if what is meant is that by which one is punished, with the preposition (*ḥarf al-jarr*) omitted. ﴿anyone from among the worlds﴾: i.e., from among the people of their own time, or from among the worlds absolutely, for they were transformed into apes and swine, and no one else was punished with the like of that.

It is narrated that a table (*sufra*) of red food descended between two clouds while they were looking at it, until it fell before them. 'Isa, peace be upon him, wept and said: "O Allah, make me among the thankful. O Allah, make it a mercy and not a disfigurement and a punishment." Then he stood, performed ablution, prayed and wept. Then he uncovered the cloth and said: "In the name of Allah, the best of providers." Behold, there was a roasted fish without scales or bones, dripping with fat; at its head was salt, at its tail was vinegar, and around it were various kinds of herbs except leek. And behold, there were five loaves of bread: on one was olives, on the second honey, on the third butter, on the fourth cheese, and on the fifth dried meat. Shim'un said: "O Spirit of Allah, is this from the food of this world or from the food of the Hereafter?" He said: "It is neither of them, but Allah, glorified and exalted, created it by His power. Eat what you have asked for, and give thanks, and Allah will increase you [in provision] and add to you of His bounty." They said: "O Spirit of Allah, if you would show us another sign besides this sign." He said: "O fish, come alive by the permission of Allah, the Exalted." It thrashed about, then he said to it: "Return as you were," and it returned roasted. Then the table flew away. Then they disobeyed after that, and they were transformed.

It was also said that it would come to them for forty days, every other day, and the poor and the rich, the young and the old would gather around it and eat until the shade began to move, and then it would fly away while they watched its shadow. No poor person ate from it without becoming rich for the rest of his life, and no sick person ate from it without being cured and never falling ill again. Then Allah, exalted, revealed to 'Isa, peace be upon him, that he should make My table for the poor and the sick, not for the rich and the healthy. The people were thrown into turmoil over this, and so eighty-three men were transformed.

It was also said that when Allah promised to send it down on this condition, they asked to be excused and said: "We do not want it," so it was not sent down. It is narrated from Mujahid that this is a parable which Allah set forth for those who demand miracles. It is also narrated from some of the Sufis that "the table" here is an expression for the realities of gnosis (*ḥaqā'iq al-ma'ārif*), for these are the nourishment of the soul just as foods are the nourishment of the body. In this case, the situation may have been that they desired realities for which they were not prepared to stand, so 'Isa, peace be upon him, said to them: "If you attain faith, then practise piety until you become capable of being made aware of them." But they did not desist from the question and persisted in it, so he asked on their behalf. Then Allah, glorified and exalted, made clear that sending it down is easy, but there is in it danger and fear of consequence: for the wayfarer (*al-sālik*), when there is revealed to him what is above his station, perhaps he cannot bear it and does not remain steady, and so he goes astray with a far going-astray. (p-151)

Commentary of al-Baydawi (*Anwar al-Tanzil*) on Surah 5, verse 116:

﴿And when Allah says, "O Jesus, son of Mary, did you say to the people, 'Take me and my mother as two gods besides Allah'?"﴾ He intends by this the rebuke and reproach of the disbelievers. "Besides Allah" (*min dun Allah*) is a qualifier (*sifah*) of "two gods," or it is a complement (*silah*) of "take me." As for the meaning of *dun* (دون, "besides"), it may signify difference (*al-mughayarah*). In that case there is an indication that worshipping Allah, glorified and exalted is He, together with worshipping other than Him is as if it were no worship at all. Whoever worships Him along with worshipping those two is as though he worshipped them and did not worship Him. Or it may signify deficiency (*al-qusur*): they did not believe that the two were independently deserving of worship, but they claimed that worshipping them leads to the worship of Allah, glorified and exalted is He. It is as if it were said: "Take me and my mother as two gods who bring you closer to Allah, glorified and exalted is He."

﴿He said, "Glory be to You"﴾ I declare You far above (*unazzihuka tanzihan*) from having any partner. ﴿It is not for me to say what is not right for me﴾ meaning: it is not befitting for me to say a statement that it is not right for me to make. ﴿If I had said it, You would have known it. You know what is in my soul, and I do not know what is in Your soul﴾ You know what I conceal in my soul just as You know what I disclose, and I do not know what You conceal of Your knowledge. His saying "in Your soul" (*fi nafsika*) is for the sake of parallelism (*al-mushakalah*). It has also been said that the intended meaning of "soul" (*nafs*) is the essence (*al-dhat*). ﴿Indeed, You are the Knower of the unseen﴾ This is a confirmation of the two statements, taken in terms of both their explicit (*mantuq*) and implicit (*mafhum*) meaning.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 5, verses 117–118:

﴿I did not say to them except what You commanded me: "Worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord."﴾ This is an explicit negation of what was questioned, after mentioning that which indicates it. ﴿That [i.e., "Worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord"]﴾ is an explicative apposition (ʿaṭf bayān) to the pronoun in "bihi" (by which), or a substitute (badal) of it. It is not a condition of the substitute that the substituted element may be omitted in all cases, lest the relative clause remain without a returning pronoun. It may also be the predicate of an implied subject, such as "huwa" (it is), or its object, such as "aʿnī" (I mean). It is not permissible for it to be a substitute of "mā amartanī bihi" (what You commanded me), because the verbal noun cannot be the object of the verb of saying; nor can "an" be an interpretive particle (mufassira), because the command is ascribed to Allah, exalted is He, and He does not say "Worship Allah, my Lord and your Lord." The verb of saying is not interpreted in this way; rather, the sentence is quoted after it. Except that the verb of saying may be interpreted as a verb of commanding, so it is as if it were said: "I did not command them except with what You commanded me, namely: Worship Allah." ﴿And I was a witness over them while I remained among them﴾, i.e., a watcher over them, preventing them from saying that and believing it, or a witness to their conditions of disbelief and faith. ﴿Then when You caused me to die﴾: by raising me to the heavens, in accordance with His saying: ﴿Indeed, I will cause you to die and raise you to Me﴾. Tawaffī means taking a thing in full, and death is a kind of it. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Allah takes the souls at the time of their death, and those that do not die during their sleep﴾. ﴿You were the Watcher over them﴾, the one observing their conditions, so You prevent whomever You wish to protect from believing it, by guiding to the proofs and alerting to them through sending messengers and revealing signs. ﴿And You are over all things Witness﴾, having knowledge of it and observing it.

﴿If You punish them, indeed they are Your servants﴾, i.e., if You punish them, You are punishing Your servants, and there is no objection to the absolute Owner regarding what He does with His dominion. This contains an indication that they deserved that, because they are Your servants and they worshipped other than You. ﴿And if You forgive them, indeed You, You are the Exalted in Might, the Wise﴾: so there is no weakness and no reproach, for You are the Capable, the Strong, over reward and punishment, who rewards and punishes only for wisdom and rightness. Indeed forgiveness is commendable for every wrongdoer. If You punish, it is justice; if You forgive, it is grace. The non-forgiveness of shirk is in accordance with the requirement of the threat (waʿīd), so there is no impossibility in it in itself, which would prevent the expression of uncertainty and conditionality with "an."

(p-152) God said: ﴿This is a day when the truthful will profit from their truthfulness.﴾ Nafi' read ﴿يَوْمَ﴾ (yawma) with a fatha, as an adverbial complement (ẓarf, an adverb of time) of "قال" (qala, "said"), and the predicate (khabar) of ﴿هَذا﴾ (hadha, "this") is omitted. Alternatively, it is an adverbial complement of a stable predicate (ẓarf mustaqarr) that functions as the predicate, and the meaning is: "What has passed of the words of Jesus is occurring on a day when truthfulness profits." It has also been said that it is a predicate but is built on the fatha because it is attached to a verb (mabni 'ala al-fath bi-idafatihi ila al-fi'l). This is not correct, because the noun that is attached to (al-mudaf ilayhi) takes i'rab (grammatical inflection). By "truthfulness" is meant truthfulness in this world, since what profits is that which occurs during the time of accountability (al-taklif). ﴿For them are gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. God is pleased with them, and they are pleased with Him. That is the great triumph.﴾ This explains the profit. ﴿To God belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth and whatever is in them, and He is over all things competent.﴾ This is a warning against the lie of the Christians and the corruption of their claim concerning the Messiah and his mother. He did not say "wa man fihinna" (and whoever is in them) but said "wa ma fihinna" (and whatever is in them), giving precedence to the rational beings (taghlib al-'uqala', giving predominance to the rational) and, following them, the non-rational ones (ghayr uli al-'aql). This informs that they are in the utmost deficiency regarding the meaning of lordship (rububiyya) and have descended from the rank of servitude (ubudiyya), as a humiliation of them and a reminder of the similarity (mujanasa) that contradicts divinity (uluhiyya). Moreover, what is used in a generic sense, encompassing all kinds, is more appropriate for the intention of generality.

From the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surah al-Ma'idah will be given the reward of ten good deeds, ten of his bad deeds will be erased, and ten degrees will be raised for him, equal to the number of every Jew and Christian who breathes in the world."
